#6366. A man using a metal detector in Germany found the biggest stash of Roman silver coins from Emperor Hadrian ever discovered

A metal detectorist discovered 934 Roman silver coins near Cologne, Germany, uncovering the country's largest known hoard from Hadrian's reign.

Oliver Riedl had already dug up 15 Roman silver coins in a field near Wesseling, south of Cologne, when his metal detector kept signaling. He immediately notified the regional heritage office.

The excavation that followed recovered 934 Roman silver denarii, about 6.8 pounds (3.1 kilograms) of silver. It is the largest coin hoard from the reign of Emperor Hadrian ever found in Germany.

The LVR Office for Archaeological Heritage Management in the Rhineland (LVR-ABR) announced the find on September 22, 2026.

Riedl, an amateur metal detectorist, was searching the field with official permission.

“For me it was clear that something bigger was lying in the ground here,” Riedl said. “So I notified the office immediately.”

The LVR-ABR‘s branch in Nideggen responded immediately and excavated the site. To study the find more closely, archaeologists lifted it in a block of soil and X-rayed it at the LVR-LandesMuseum Bonn‘s restoration workshop.

Dr. Erich Claßen is the state archaeologist and head of the LVR-ABR.

“This makes it the largest coin hoard from this period in Germany, and worldwide it is the fifth largest,” Claßen explained.

The latest coin in the hoard was minted in AD 124 or 125. The archaeologists think the coins were buried in the second quarter of the second century, under Hadrian, who ruled from AD 117 to 138.

Most of the coins date to the Flavian emperors, who ruled from AD 69 to 96. Among them is a denarius of Domitian, the last emperor of that dynasty.

The oldest coin was struck in 148 BC, during the Roman Republic. It was more than 270 years old when it went into the ground.

The fortune was probably assembled around AD 100 and buried on purpose decades later.

In that period, the Rhine formed the frontier of the Roman province of Lower Germany. Its defenses, the Lower German Limes, ran about 250 miles (400 kilometers) from south of Bonn to the North Sea, according to UNESCO.

From the late first century BC, that frontier protected the Roman Empire for more than 450 years. Its remains include legionary fortresses, forts, watchtowers, roads and towns.

Dr. Rahel Otte, a research associate at the LVR-ABR, studied the coins.

“At that time, an ordinary soldier in the legion earned 300 denarii a year,” Otte noted.

About half of that pay was withheld for food and equipment. To save 934 denarii, a legionary would have had to set aside all of his available money for about six years, Otte calculated.

Who amassed this considerable fortune remains unclear. The owner may have lived on one of the Roman country estates in the surrounding area.

“We can of course only speculate about the motives, but very probably someone wanted to keep this money safe. After all, there were no banks back then,” Claßen observed.

Why the silver stayed in the ground is also unknown. The owner may have died without passing on what they knew about the coins.

The soil block also held fragments of a buried clay pot and remains of straw.

“The coins were probably originally buried in a pot padded with straw,” Otte explained.

Years of farming had destroyed the pot and scattered the coins through the topsoil.

“But in our investigations we were able to find and recover all of the coins,” Otte stressed.

“Mr. Riedl really behaved in an exemplary way,” Claßen remarked. “Thanks to his care, we were able to recover the hoard properly and completely,” he added.

Under the monument protection law of North Rhine-Westphalia, the hoard now belongs to the state. Because Riedl acted lawfully, the state ministry responsible for heritage will give him a reward.

Metal detecting in the Rhineland requires a permit from the heritage authorities and the landowner’s consent, whatever a person is searching for.

Applicants first attend an information session run by the LVR-ABR and mark the areas they want to search on a map. Detectors are allowed only on arable fields, not on meadows or in forests.

Simon Matzerath chairs the West and South German Association for Archaeological Research. About 300 archaeologists from across Germany saw the hoard at the association’s annual conference in Bonn.

“The private use of metal detectors can be an incredible support for science if everyone follows the rules, but unfortunately we also often have to deal with so-called illegal digs,” Matzerath said.

The hoard will go on public display for the first time at the LVR-LandesMuseum Bonn.

The information was obtained from the LVR Office for Archaeological Heritage Management in the Rhineland.

#6365. A virus found in one out of ten patients in China is carried by a tick species that is spreading across the US

Researchers in China identified a new tick-borne virus, ALTNV, linked to fever and more severe illness when combined with another virus.

Researchers in China found a newly identified tick-borne virus in 10.4 percent of 3,163 patients they tested. The virus, called Asian longhorned tick nairovirus (ALTNV), also turned up in ticks collected from 15 provinces.

Patients infected with ALTNV alone recovered. Among 38 patients also infected with the virus behind severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome (SFTS), seven died.

The tick species that carried ALTNV most often, the Asian longhorned tick, has spread across parts of the United States. The Chinese study tested only patients and ticks in China, so it does not show whether the virus is present in U.S. ticks.

The work was led by researchers at the State Key Laboratory of Pathogen and Biosecurity in Beijing, with Xiao-Ai Zhang as first author. They reported it in September 2026 in a letter titled “A Zoonotic Orthonairovirus from Febrile Patients in China.”

Their starting point was a gap in diagnosis. More than 30 percent of patients clinically diagnosed with SFTS test negative for Dabie bandavirus (DBV), the virus that causes the disease.

The team screened 3,163 patients with fever and a history of tick exposure. They looked for ALTNV genetic material or IgM antibodies, which the immune system makes early in an infection.

Among patients who had tested negative for DBV, 15.1 percent tested positive for ALTNV.

ALTNV belongs to the genus Orthonairovirus in the family Nairoviridae. Its proteins share less than 80 percent of their amino acids with other species in that genus.

The researchers described 56 patients with ALTNV alone. Fatigue affected 84 percent of them, and 80 percent had gastrointestinal symptoms.

Low platelet counts, known as thrombocytopenia, appeared in 38 percent. Raised levels of the liver enzymes called aminotransferases appeared in 36 percent.

All of these patients recovered without lasting effects.

In the 38 patients carrying both ALTNV and DBV, coinfection was linked to more severe illness. Respiratory symptoms affected 61 percent of them, compared with 38 percent of patients with DBV alone.

Kidney impairment affected 84 percent of the coinfected patients, compared with 66 percent. Seven of them, or 18.4 percent, died.

The two viruses circulate in the same areas and share a tick vector. The authors call for better tests to tell these tick-borne viruses apart where SFTS is common.

The team also tested 47,428 ticks gathered across 15 Chinese provinces. ALTNV genetic material turned up in 1.29 percent of them.

The Asian longhorned tick, Haemaphysalis longicornis, carried the virus most often, at 1.75 percent.

In laboratory experiments, the species passed ALTNV to mice.

Outside Asia, this tick can reduce production in dairy cattle by 25 percent in some regions of New Zealand and Australia, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) noted in 2018.

New Jersey was the first U.S. state to report the tick, on a sheep in August 2017, according to the CDC.

A single female can reproduce without mating. As a result, hundreds or thousands of ticks can build up on one animal or in one area.

Ben Beard, Ph.D., was then deputy director of the CDC’s Division of Vector-Borne Diseases.

“The full public health and agricultural impact of this tick discovery and spread is unknown,” Beard said in 2018.

By October 2025, the U.S. Department of Agriculture had documented the tick in 21 states, with Kansas the most recent.

There, it was found on a dog in Franklin County, according to the Kansas Department of Agriculture and the Kansas Department of Health and Environment (KDHE).

The ticks have been collected from New York south to Georgia and west to Missouri. They are not competent vectors of the bacterium behind Lyme disease, the USDA’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) states.

In cattle, the species can transmit Theileria orientalis Ikeda, a parasite responsible for bovine theileriosis. U.S. ticks passed it to cattle in the laboratory, and it has been detected in ticks collected in the field.

In 2025, the Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station (CAES) reported the first evidence in the U.S. of a longhorned tick infected with Ehrlichia chaffeensis. This bacterium causes human monocytic ehrlichiosis.

Dr. Goudarz Molaei is a research scientist and medical entomologist at the CAES and an adjunct associate professor at the Yale School of Public Health.

“A rigorous program in mitigating risks should include expanded tick surveillance programs, strict measures to inspect animals, plants, and other imported materials at ports of entry, accurate and proper identification of exotic ticks and pathogens, effective eradication and prevention measures, and the ability to test exotic ticks for both native and nonnative pathogens,” Molaei said.

In 2019, an Asian longhorned tick in Virginia was found to be infected with Bourbon virus, the Kansas agencies noted.

The study was published in the journal New England Journal of Medicine.

#6364. Curiosity captures a martian dawn

The morning Sun casts a hazy glow over Mars’ Mount Sharp, lighting up distant wind-carved rock formations known as yardangs. This scene is cropped from a six-image panorama captured by the Mastcam on NASA’s Curiosity rover at 8:30 a.m. local time on Aug. 11, 2026, the mission’s 4,982nd sol (martian day). Mount Sharp, formally Aeolis Mons, stands 3.4 miles (5.5 km) tall at the center of Mars’ 96-mile-wide (154 km) Gale Crater. Since 2014, Curiosity has climbed roughly 0.6 mile (1 km) up its stratified slopes, reading each new layer like a chapter of martian geology.

The mountain’s lowest, oldest layers likely formed from sediment deposited by lakes and streams that have long since vanished. This photo is the most detailed view to date of the much younger yardang layer. Of particular interest is the fact that the color and orientation of the yardangs don’t match the surrounding material. Scientists think these features could have been built up from volcanic ash that settled after a nearby eruption, and was then carved away by the wind. Curiosity should reach the yardangs’ base in 2027, where its instruments will help uncover how the layer formed.

Brooks Mendenhall is a staff writer at Astronomy, based in Chattanooga, Tennessee, fueled by an unending curiosity about the universe. A former classroom teacher, he has a knack for breaking down complex concepts for a wide audience.

Live Science readers respond to a recent poll about whether they'd visit the Red Planet even with potential health risks.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For centuries, Mars has been seen as a potential place for future human settlements. But long-duration space travel comes with serious risks to astronauts' health, including those resulting from cosmic radiation and the effects of microgravity.

A new study found that rats that were exposed to radiation similar to what astronauts might encounter during a Mars mission developed more scar tissue around their hearts' small blood vessels compared with a control group. Although the findings haven't been validated in humans, the results contribute to growing concerns about the potential effects of long-haul space missions on astronauts' health.

Given these new findings, Live Science asked its readers whether they'd travel to the Red Planet, despite these potential health risks. Over 240 readers weighed in, with 65% picking "No, I don't think the risks are worth it."

Interestingly enough, the comments reflect a slightly different trend. One reader wrote, "Any pioneers who travel to Mars will be facing the prospect of death and never coming back. Even if they make it back, there are any number of health issues that could come up. These risks have not stopped people from exploring throughout human history. The bigger question is who to send?"

Other commenters echoed this sentiment, with another reader posting, "Explorers in the past have always been exposed to unusual risks; without the risk takers we would still believe the world is flat."

Beyond the feelings that Mars will be explored anyway, despite the health risks, other commenters highlighted the cost of these missions, with one reader stating, "Sending flesh water balloons to Mars is ridiculous. For the cost of one human on Mars, we could literally probe the entire solar system and map/sample/rove every planet and every major Moon."

Others highlighted the mental and emotional cost of a trip to Mars. "As a devoted sci-fi fan for decades, I always wished I could go into space," another reader noted. "Now that I am 77 years old, I realize I would miss the outdoors. The wind and trees, the birdsong and sweet grass under my feet would be a devastating loss. Let the brave explorers go instead. Life is too brief to leave this planet for the uncertainty and dangers of space travel."

Do you agree with these readers? Let us know your thoughts in the comments!

#6362. Arctic winter sea ice is being overestimated by climate models

Ancient algae preserved in Arctic seafloor mud suggest climate models overestimate winter sea ice, pointing to less ice in the decades ahead.

Arctic sea ice loss usually gets told as a summer story, counting down to the first ice-free summer. Yet climate models disagree most about winter ice.

Together, they simulate nearly a million square kilometers too much March ice – about 386,000 square miles, close to Texas and New Mexico combined.

A new study used traces of algae buried in 6,000-year-old seafloor mud to grade 27 climate models.

The corrected projections show about a million square kilometers less winter ice than before, in every coming decade and under every emissions path.

Crystal Fu of the Scott Polar Research Institute led the work with Matthew Osman at the University of Cambridge, and Marco Aquino-López of CIMAT in Mexico.

The numbers are model projections re-weighted by evidence from the past, not new measurements of today’s ice.

In an interview with Earth.com, Fu compared the missing ice to a country.

“A million square kilometers is a huge amount of sea ice to go missing – that’s roughly 4x the size of the UK,” she said.

Winter ice matters because it’s a lid. Open water in the Arctic winter releases heat and moisture into the air.

That release has been linked to colder winters and heavier snow across Eurasia and North America. It has also been linked to shifts in storm tracks and extreme rain in the Mediterranean.

In March 2025, the Arctic’s annual maximum was the lowest on record.

Yet the models’ biggest disagreements and biggest errors fall in March, not September, and most of the testing has gone into summer.

Fu’s team wanted an exam the models couldn’t have been tuned to pass.

Between 5,000 and 7,000 years ago, a wobble in Earth’s orbit gave the Arctic more summer sunlight. The extra sunlight warmed the region and reduced its sea ice.

The extra heating was comparable in size to what future greenhouse gases are expected to add.

Algae that live inside sea ice leave a distinctive molecule behind, and algae that live in open water leave others.

The ratio of the two in a layer of seafloor mud records how much ice covered that spot. Fu’s team compiled 46 such records from sediment cores across the Arctic, the largest set of its kind.

“What really struck us was just how much information is preserved in tiny traces of algae buried in mud across the Arctic seafloor,” she said.

The team converted the 27 models’ ancient Arctic ice simulations into molecular ratios for comparison with the sediment records.

That let the models be compared with the cores on equal terms. Each model got a weight based on how well it matched, with related models sharing credit.

Weighted that way, the models’ average March ice for the recent past matched the satellite record. The bias of nearly a million square kilometers disappeared.

The range of disagreement shrank by about 6.3 million square kilometers (2.4 million square miles), or 85%. The remaining range was comparable to ordinary year-to-year swings.

The ancient records turned out to be the sharper test. Weighting by the mid-Holocene alone corrected the models more than weighting by 1950 to 1999 did.

The same weights applied to the models’ futures lowered the projected March ice by 4% to 6% for the 2090s, under low, middle and high emissions alike.

Fu noted that the cause of the ancient warming doesn’t change the lesson.

“It doesn’t matter if the warming is natural variation or caused by human activity: if it warms, sea ice is going to melt,” she said.

In the Barents Sea, the Greenland Sea and the Labrador Sea, the weighted maps put the winter ice edge farther north than the unweighted models do.

The shift reaches 5.5 degrees of latitude, about 380 miles (610 kilometers).

Asked by Earth.com where winter sea ice was most vulnerable, Osman pointed to the Barents Sea.

“The Barents Sea, north of Norway and Russia, is probably the place to watch most closely right now,” he said.

The Greenland and Labrador Seas, farther south, are the next places to watch, Osman said.

More ice loss there could affect marine wildlife, shipping, the Atlantic’s circulation and the stability of the Greenland ice sheet, he added.

The projections assume the ice will keep responding to warming the way it did 6,000 years ago and in the 20th century.

The weighting improved the combined projection, but it did not explain why individual models produced different amounts of ice.

Links between winter ice and weather farther south also need confirming. Under high emissions, the weighted models suggest late-winter snowfall over southeast Greenland may be underestimated by more than 30%.

Winter and spring rain in the Mediterranean may be twice what the standard models project, which would raise flood risk there.

Fu said exactly how the Arctic changes will affect Europe’s winters is still being studied.

Earlier work tied a weaker polar vortex and cold snaps to a bare Barents Sea, but those links still need verifying.

Osman said the bigger payoff lies beyond sea ice.

Decades of records of ancient climates can be paired with the right mathematics to test climate models and narrow their projections, he said.

The snowfall and rainfall estimates suggest that ancient climate records could help refine projections beyond sea ice, although those results still need further testing.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Geoscience.

#6361. Food contains thousands of overlooked chemicals. This physicist is mapping them

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By Tina Hesman Saey, Mandana Tadayon and Anna Mattson

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Computational physicist Giulia Menichetti is looking for “dark matter” in our food. In addition to known macronutrients, vitamins and minerals, the things we eat contain a whole world of natural chemicals we have no idea about. And those chemicals may affect our health.

“They have the ability to interact, to bind to human proteins, to modulate our microbiome,” says Menichetti of Harvard Medical School. “We want to leverage this to talk more and more about the role of food and nutrition in human health.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Menichetti leads Foodome, a project to map our food’s full chemical complexity. Her team uses AI to mine scientific papers for every chemical compound that has ever been linked to a food. She singles out ones that haven’t been tracked by epidemiological studies — the “nutritional dark matter.” So far, her team has cataloged about 140,000 molecules.

When one hears about chemicals in food, they might initially think of artificial additives. Her team addresses those, but she’s also interested in naturally occurring chemicals. Take garlic, for example. Foodome has cataloged almost 7,000 different molecules in raw garlic alone. Some of these compounds have been investigated for health effects, but some are entirely new.

Foodome is still mining the scientific literature for these molecules and building out databases. Eventually, Menichetti would like AI to be able to predict how all these food molecules interact together and in the human body.

“There is a legacy of chemical complexity that comes from organisms that are all around us,” she says. “Food is part of that. It is actually our way to interact with our environment. We need to study it better.”

#6359. Taking cold showers is good for your health and also the environment, according to a new study

In trials with 719 adults, people who took cold showers at least 70% of the time reported 26% fewer illness days and 31% fewer days off work.

Giving up a warm shower sounds simple until it’s time to step under the water. In a Swiss study, plenty of people signed up to try it, but many stopped early.

Those who kept going reported fewer days feeling sick and fewer days off work over 12 weeks. Their showers also came with a small estimated drop in carbon emissions, although extra encouragement did little to help people keep the habit.

Lena Glaser, a psychologist and psychotherapist at the University of Basel, knows from her clinical work how hard people can find change.

For her doctoral dissertation in the Faculty of Psychology, she studied whether a habit is easier to keep when people can fit it into their day and get something out of it.

“We need a more empathetic approach if we want people to change their behavior,” Glaser said.

Cars, food, and recycling usually come up when people discuss their climate impact, Glaser said. Yet European and U.S. energy agencies put water heating at about 15% to 25% of the energy used in homes in wealthy countries, a use that gets much less attention.

“Taking a cold shower isn’t exactly pleasant, but it’s a small change to make,” she said. “After all, we shower anyway.”

Ice baths and cold plunges have made cold water a popular health topic, but the evidence remains limited. A 2025 review found 11 trials in healthy adults, only one of which tested showers.

That Dutch trial, published in PLOS ONE, asked people to finish a warm shower with up to 90 seconds of cold water. They reported 29% less sick leave than a comparison group, but no fewer days of illness.

Glaser brought together results from three trials she and her colleagues ran between late 2019 and mid-2024. In all, 719 adults took part.

To join, people had to speak German, be healthy, and be between 18 and 65, with no cold-shower habit already in place. Pregnancy ruled people out, as did conditions such as severe asthma or severe heart disease that cold might make worse.

The instructions were straightforward: turn the tap to its coldest setting and stay under the water for two to five minutes. Once a month, volunteers filled out surveys about days with cold, flu, or other symptoms and days they’d missed work because of illness.

Two of the trials asked everyone to try cold showers, which left no randomly chosen comparison group. So for this analysis, Glaser’s team put people who showered cold at least 70% of the time in one group: 459 volunteers, or about three in five.

Before the trials, volunteers reported about three days of illness and one day off work each month. Over 12 weeks, regular cold showerers reported 26% fewer illness days and 31% fewer days off work than everyone else.

The difference was modest for any one person. The team’s calculation put it at one fewer day of illness among 16 people taking cold showers for a week.

The gap stayed similar from the first month to the last. Cold showerers also scored slightly higher on a standard well-being questionnaire, but their physical well-being scores did not differ reliably.

Skin health ratings were much the same in both groups, with complaints including dry or itchy skin and a few slips in the shower. No one reported a serious problem.

The team looked more closely at quitting among 586 people in the two later trials. Only 217, or 37%, kept taking cold showers for all 12 weeks.

People were most likely to quit in the early weeks. They became less likely to stop as time went on.

“That suggests people gradually get used to it,” Glaser said.

Women were more likely to stop than men. About 32% of women reached the end, compared with about 47% of men.

In the second trial, some volunteers watched short monthly videos giving them reasons to continue, from personal benefits to climate action. None of the four versions helped people last longer than basic instructions did.

Weekly emails didn’t help either. Of the 71 volunteers who received five emails with confidence-building texts and videos in the third trial, just 10 finished the 12 weeks, the lowest completion rate of any group.

The researchers suggested that weekly messages may have made a personal choice feel like an obligation. That could weaken people’s motivation instead of helping.

“When people see a personal benefit from changing their behavior and don’t feel that they’re giving something up or missing out, they’re more motivated to stick with it,” Glaser said.

The energy calculation started with a five-minute shower using 12 gallons (45 liters) of water. Taking that water from a warm 104°F (40°C) down to 59°F (15°C) would save about 1.3 kilowatt-hours.

That worked out to an estimated 33 pounds (15 kilograms) less carbon dioxide per volunteer over the study. Using the team’s comparison, that’s about as much as a car releases on a 62-mile (100-kilometer) trip.

For someone keeping up the habit for a year, the team estimated savings of about 143 pounds (65 kilograms). That equals about 2% to 3% of an average person’s annual household carbon footprint in wealthy European countries.

The researchers didn’t put meters in people’s homes. They assumed a daily five-minute shower and used average emissions figures for German and Swiss energy, so the savings in a particular home would depend on its water heater.

The volunteers averaged about 26 years old, and roughly two-thirds were women. They also chose to take on the challenge, so they were probably more motivated than most people.

Everyone knew which group they were in, and the researchers relied on survey answers for both shower habits and illness. No medical tests confirmed whether people were sick.

There’s another complication: people who managed to keep showering cold might have differed from those who gave up. Comparing those groups cannot tell us whether cold water itself made anyone less likely to get sick.

The researchers don’t know who carried on after the 12 weeks ended. Nor did they track whether volunteers went on to use more energy elsewhere because they felt they’d already done their bit, a possibility people have also raised about recycling.

For Glaser, keeping a habit needn’t mean doing it exactly the same way every day.

“The water doesn’t have to be equally cold every day,” Glaser said. “We don’t feel equally brave every day, and that’s okay.”

One question for future studies, Glaser suggested, is whether this small change could make bigger ones feel more manageable. Would people who get used to cold showers become more willing to change what they eat or fly less?

The full study is available as a doctoral dissertation through edoc, the University of Basel’s open-access repository.

#6358. Pumping hydrogen in and out of a deep fault may steady it rather than shake it loose

Computer models of a natural hydrogen deposit in Albania suggest that pumping hydrogen in and out each year could leave its fault steadier.

Pumping gas in and out of a fault deep underground sounds like a good way to make it slip. For a natural hydrogen deposit under a mine in Albania, a new modeling study suggests the opposite.

With the right injection depth, each year of filling and emptying left the fault less likely to slip than the year before.

That points to a new job for hydrogen pockets too small to be worth mining. They could become storage sites for hydrogen made somewhere else.

Lei Hou, an associate professor at the China-UK Low Carbon College of Shanghai Jiao Tong University, designed the study with his colleague Zhengxin Zhang. Fengshou Zhang of Tongji University and Derek Elsworth of Penn State were among the co-authors.

Everything they report comes from computer simulations – no hydrogen has been pumped into this fault yet.

An energy system that runs partly on hydrogen needs somewhere to keep huge amounts of it for months at a time. Tanks at the surface can’t do that at scale, so the gas has to go underground.

The usual candidates are caverns cut into thick salt, porous rock soaked with salty water, and old oil and gas fields. None of them, the authors wrote, comes with direct proof that it can store hydrogen in particular.

A natural hydrogen deposit does. If the gas has built up there over geological time, the rock has already shown it can keep hydrogen in.

Many such deposits are too weak to sell. Their natural flow typically falls at least ten times short of what commercial production needs, and the authors expect most future finds of natural hydrogen to fall short too.

Hundreds of these sites are already on record worldwide, including a mine in northern Ontario, and the list keeps growing.

The deposit the team modeled lies under the Bulqizë chromite mine. In 2024, other researchers reported in Science that the mine releases at least 220 tons (200 metric tons) of hydrogen a year, one of the largest natural flows ever recorded.

Gas sampled there is 84 percent hydrogen. The gas collects in a fault zone inside slabs of ancient ocean crust. The fault tilts at 80 degrees, almost straight down, and reaches as deep as about 3 miles (5 km). Temperatures along it run from about 104°F to 320°F (40°C to 160°C).

That heat helps. The main microbial routes that consume hydrogen underground work best below about 104°F (40°C), and the methane in the mine’s gas appears to come from rock chemistry rather than microbes.

Other teams have looked for large deposits beneath mountain ranges. Bulqizë is one of the best-studied deposits, and its steep, deep fault makes it one of the hardest places to store hydrogen safely.

Stored hydrogen can disappear in three ways. It can dissolve into underground water, microbes can consume it, or it can react with carbon in the rock to make methane.

The team gave each one generous assumptions, so real losses should be smaller. In the simulations, about 1 percent of the stored gas dissolved into water, and most of it came back out when the gas was pumped up again.

The reaction with carbon took less than 0.3 percent, and microbes took even less.

Added together, the losses stayed under 2 percent. That fits the deposit’s own history. It holds an estimated 5,500 to 55,000 tons (5,000 to 50,000 metric tons) of hydrogen and has kept releasing gas with no sign of running dry.

Underground oil and gas work has been linked to earthquakes before, so the team tested where along the fault to inject. They ran 72 combinations of depth, pumping rate, and how easily gas moves through the rock.

In the model, injecting near the top, where the fault meets the rock layer sealing it, pushed the fault toward slipping every time. Shallow and middle depths were safe only at the slowest rate, which stored too little. The very bottom caused trouble too, because gas piled up in the tight rock there.

Injecting at about 14,500 feet (4,400 meters) worked best. Under the best plans, the team estimates the fault could hold roughly 12 to 17 billion cubic feet (350 to 480 million cubic meters) of gas, depending on the rock.

That’s about as much as the fault held naturally, and in some setups more.

The team then ran ten simulated years. Hydrogen went in from April to September and came out from October to March, at about 26 million cubic feet (750,000 cubic meters) a day.

That pace held for the full decade. And the fault’s slip risk during each filling season fell further every year, because the moving gas evened out the pressure inside it.

In an interview with Earth.com, Hou said the team had started from the opposite worry, since any engineering in a fault zone calls for caution. “What surprised us was that the cycling itself helped.”

“This stabilizing effect is not automatic – it depends on choosing the right injection depth,” Hou added.

Some processes are missing from the model. It doesn’t capture how shifting stress changes the rock’s ability to pass gas, and its grid may miss fine detail near the wells.

It also leaves out rock fatigue from repeated pressure swings, which could change the fault’s behavior beyond ten years.

Hou was asked when a site like this could store hydrogen commercially. “I cannot give you a date, and I would be cautious of anyone who does,” he told Earth.com.

Field trials and engineering costs will set the timeline, he said. The appeal, in his view, is economic. An explored deposit too weak to develop currently leaves its operator two choices: suspend the project or abandon it. Storage would add a third.

What the fault would do after a decade of cycling remains an open question. Until hydrogen is pumped into a real fault in a field trial, the steadying effect exists only in simulations.

The full study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

The surest way to get a scratch from a feline is to go for a forbidden tummy rub. But why do cats hate being touched on their bellies?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Dogs typically love belly rubs and will roll on their backs to get more. With cats, it's a different story: Most are visibly uncomfortable when someone touches their belly, and the same applies to their feet and tail.

When a cat is petted in these areas, its body language often changes. "They might do a quick head turn, looking at your hand, or they might start moving away from you or wiggling around a lot, basically trying to get away from the petting," Mikel Delgado, a cat behaviorist and senior research scientist at Purdue University, told Live Science in an email. "If these early warning signs are ignored, they might escalate to biting, hissing or scratching."

But why do cats dislike it so much when humans touch these specific areas?

Although there has been little formal research into this question, animal behavior experts proposed a few ideas for why cats don't like to be touched in certain areas.

"Cats are prey animals as well as predators and so they can be very protective of areas that are particularly vulnerable to injury during attack, such as the belly area," Sarah Ellis, head of cat mental well-being and behavior at the cat welfare charity International Cat Care, told Live Science in an email.

A cat's belly houses vital organs ‪—‬ such as the liver, stomach and intestines ‪—‬ without the protective bony cage that the ribs provide for the heart and lungs. Although cats have evolved a special feature called the "primordial pouch" —‬ basically a flap of loose skin and fat on their belly —‬ which provides a little extra padding to protect vital organs during fights, most cats still feel threatened when humans touch or rub their belly.

Cats have extra padding on their stomachs to protect their organs.

Dogs have a similar anatomy to cats, but they have to worry less about falling prey to larger animals. Cats, meanwhile, can be hunted by dogs, urban coyotes, and even birds such as hawks and owls, making it natural for them to be protective of their bellies.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

The tail is also a vulnerable area for cats. "When a cat is chased by another animal, including other cats, the tail is often the part of the cat's body that is closest to touch," Ellis said, "and the risk of being bitten at the base of the tail is high." Therefore, cats may be skittish about having their tail stroked.

When it comes to foot rubs, there are two possible explanations for why most cats hate them. First, a cat's paws are essential in threatening situations. Running away from danger is a cat's preferred survival strategy, and they rely on their paws as a means of escape, Ellis explained. If they can't run away, "a cat may resort to repelling any threats through swiping and scratching and it needs its paws free to do so," she said. "It is therefore predisposed to not enjoy having its paws restricted in any way."

Another reason could be that cats' paws are very sensitive. They have wrist whiskers (also known as "carpal vibrissae") and toe pads that are sensitive to various types of stimuli, like pressure and heat, Delgado said, "so it's not surprising that many cats are sensitive about having their feet touched."

If you're interacting with a cat, it's generally a good idea to stick to the areas where most cats like to be petted: the base of their ears, around their cheeks and under their chin. These areas are rich in scent glands, and cats tend to rub them against other cats they are friends with, Delgado explained. So essentially, cats like being petted in those areas because "they treat us as they do other cats," Delgado said.

But some cats go against the grain. "I've had a few who enjoyed belly rubs," Delgado said. Others enjoy having their tail stroked briefly and show their pleasure "by pushing their rump into the hand of the petter and holding their tail up in the air," Ellis said. (This behavior is sometimes called "elevator butt.")

As puzzling as it may be to humans, these varied preferences are a reminder that "each cat is an individual," Delgado said. Positive responses to petting of the belly, feet or tail can also signal close bonding to a human, Ellis said.

She advises people to "always take the cat's lead, learn what each individual cat likes and dislikes and respect these preferences."

How much of a cat fan are you? Find out by taking our cat quiz!

She learned how to edit scientific papers in a stint as a chemistry copyeditor, before moving on to a medical writer role at a healthcare company. Writing for doctors and experts has its rewards, but Clarissa wanted to communicate with a wider audience, which naturally led her to freelance health and science writing. Her work has also appeared in Medscape, HealthCentral and Medical News Today.

#6356. The Sky This Week from November 6 to 13: Venus in the spotlight

Friday, November 6The waning Moon leaves us with perfect skies for deep-sky observing. Let’s kick off the week with a bright planetary nebula in Aquarius: NGC 7293, commonly known as the Helix Nebula.

Despite its impressive magnitude of 7.3, the Helix presents a challenge: It is a broad 13’ across, which spreads its light over a relatively large part of sky, lowering its overall surface brightness. That said, you can still find the Helix in large binoculars or any small scope, tucked into southeastern Aquarius, roughly 7.7° southwest of magnitude 3.3 Skat (Delta [δ] Aquarii). If you turn south around 7 P.M. local time, find Skat to the upper right of bright Fomalhaut in Piscis Austrinus, then scan to its lower right, toward 5th-magnitude 66 Aqr. That star lies about halfway between Skat and the Helix Nebula.

Once you’ve located the Helix, the more magnification you can turn on it, the better. Larger amateur scopes will start to show structure in the ring of glowing gas surrounding the central white dwarf, with the northern and southern edges glowing brighter than the eastern and western sides. That gas was once part of the central star, which puffed up and blew away its outer layers as it aged. Sunrise: 6:35 A.M. Sunset: 4:52 P.M. Moonrise: 3:56 A.M. Moonset: 3:16 P.M. Moon Phase: Waning crescent (5%)

Saturday, November 7Venus is our (morning) star of the week, capturing attention above the eastern horizon before sunrise. This morning, the Moon passes 1.1° due south of Earth’s sister planet at 7 A.M. EST.

You can easily catch the pair an hour before sunrise, some 6° high in the east and climbing as the sky begins to brighten. Magnitude –4.5 Venus blazes to the upper left of the delicate crescent Moon, whose western limb is just barely lit as the Sun sets across the lunar nearside. Look for earthshine on the already-shadowed portion of Luna’s face, as sunlight bouncing off Earth lights it up.

Near Venus is another bright light: This is Spica, Virgo’s alpha star, shining at magnitude 1.0 and also lingering in the morning twilight. This morning it lies 1.3° northeast of Venus, with the planet and star roughly side by side above the horizon. Use this view as an anchor point: By the 10th, Venus will have moved to stand due west of this star and will be located to its upper right.

Sunrise: 6:36 A.M. Sunset: 4:51 P.M. Moonrise: 5:01 A.M. Moonset: 3:40 P.M. Moon Phase: Waning crescent (1%)

Sunday, November 8Rising with the stars of western Leo shortly before midnight, bright Jupiter and its Galilean moons put on a show early this morning, better visible the farther east you’re located.

Jupiter is just under 5° northwest (to the upper right) of Regulus as they rise in the east. Fainter Mars stands roughly 3° above Jupiter. You’ll want your telescope trained on the gas giant soon after rising to catch the show, which begins at 1:29 A.M. EST as a shadow appears on the planet’s eastern limb. This is Io’s shadow — but don’t be fooled by the positions of the moons you see in your scope. The moon closest to Jupiter on the east is Callisto, while the moon just east of that is Io, whose shadow we see. Ganymede lies farthest east, while Europa is currently hidden behind the planet in an occultation. The latter appears from behind the eastern limb about 1:54 A.M. EST, not long before Callisto reaches the planet and begins a transit at 2:07 A.M. EST.

Keep an eye on Io and Europa: Io passes north of Europa at 2:23 A.M. EST, then heads into its own transit about 2:42 A.M. EST. Now the race is on, as Io approaches and then catches up with Callisto as the two moons transit, passing Callisto and moving west of it within half an hour. The two moons and Io’s shadow continue to transit until 3:45 A.M. EST, when Io’s shadow leaves the western limb, and Io takes about an hour and a quarter longer before egress. Callisto continues trundling along, finally finishing its transit about 5:51 A.M. CST, with the sky now starting to brighten with twilight in the Midwest.

Sunrise: 6:37 A.M. Sunset: 4:50 P.M. Moonrise: 6:07 A.M. Moonset: 4:08 P.M. Moon Phase: New

Monday, November 9New Moon occurs at 2:02 A.M. EST. Dark skies make tonight the perfect opportunity to try spotting Comet 161P/Hartley-IRAS, still nearly 50° above the western horizon two hours after sunset.

Glowing around 10th magnitude, the comet is currently located in far northern Aquila, near the Eagle’s border with Sagitta the Arrow. You can use Aquila’s bright luminary, Altair, to guide your way — the comet floats 7.7° north-northeast of this star. A closer but fainter guide is 4th-magnitude Alpha (α) Sagittae, just 2.3° north of the comet’s position tonight. Even a small scope will nab you the comet, but larger apertures will yield better views. Under high magnification, look at the comet’s southern side, which should be sharper as it plows into the solar wind.

Not far from Hartley-IRAS’ position is the famous Coathanger asterism, located in Vulpecula the Fox. Cataloged as Collinder 399, you’ll find it roughly 5° northwest of the comet’s position, or about 4° northwest of Alpha Sge. Visible in binoculars or any telescope (in this case, lower magnification is better), you’ll immediately see why this star pattern bears its name. It looks exactly like its namesake, with a line of stars bisected by a small curve extending to the south. At the Coathanger’s eastern edge lies the open cluster NGC 6802.

Sunrise: 6:38 A.M. Sunset: 4:49 P.M. Moonrise: 7:12 A.M. Moonset: 4:40 P.M. Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (1%)

Tuesday, November 10The waxing crescent Moon passes 0.3° south of Antares at midnight EST, although the pair is not visible at that time. You can catch our satellite setting in the west around sunset, although it will likely disappear before Antares pops out of the twilight — that will likely happen only shortly before the star itself sets as well.

Instead, challenge yourself with a different type of observation: picking up Saturn’s moon Iapetus, which tonight reaches greatest eastern elongation 9.4’ east of the ringed planet. The two-toned moon is tidally locked to its parent world, which means it rotates in time with its orbit. At eastern elongation, Iapetus’ darker hemisphere faces earthward, reducing the moon’s magnitude to nearly 12. This, combined with its distance from Saturn, makes it more of a challenge to find, but you can give it a try if you’ve got a larger scope.

Try around 9 P.M. local time when Saturn is highest, some 50° above the southern horizon. It’s the brightest point of light in this region of the sky, hanging just below Pisces and to the far upper left of Fomalhaut, the brightest star in Piscis Austrinus (much closer to the horizon). Even if you can’t locate Iapetus or don’t have a large scope, Saturn is magnificent through a telescope. Its disk spans 19” and its rings are roughly 43” across, showing off their southern side. You should definitely spot its largest and brightest moon, mid-8th-magnitude Titan, just over 2’ west of the planet. Depending on your scope and when you look, you may also spot at least three other moons: 10th-magnitude Tethys, Dione, and Rhea, closer to the planet. Tethys lies to Saturn’s west, while Rhea and Dione are to the east.

Sunrise: 6:39 A.M. Sunset: 4:48 P.M. Moonrise: 8:15 A.M. Moonset: 5:19 P.M. Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (4%)

Wednesday, November 11Venus reaches a stationary point among the stars of Virgo at 10 A.M. EST. This brings its retrograde (westward) motion to an end; after today, Venus will begin moving eastward or prograde through the sky, swinging north of Spica.

You can easily catch the bright planet in the eastern sky before dawn. Venus’ brightness has increased over just the past few days, and it now blazes at magnitude –4.7. An hour before sunrise, you’ll easily spot it alongside Spica, standing just to the star’s upper right. Both are 10° high and rising as dawn approaches. Check out Venus through a telescope: its disk shows off a crescent phase just 10% lit, but stretches an impressive 53” in the sky.

Also just becoming visible at this time is Mercury, barely 1.5° above the horizon and glowing at magnitude 1.2. See if you can locate it about 13° east (to the lower left) of Venus, although you’ll need a particularly flat horizon free of trees, buildings, and lights. Mercury, too, rises as twilight brightens, which may make the planet harder to see in the growing light. Try scanning for it with binoculars, although make sure to put them away well before sunrise from your location, which may differ from the time given below.

Sunrise: 6:41 A.M. Sunset: 4:47 P.M. Moonrise: 9:15 A.M. Moonset: 6:05 P.M. Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (8%)

Thursday, November 12The constellation Perseus is famous for its bright Double Cluster, but these two open clusters aren’t the only groups of young stars in the Hero worth viewing. Today, let’s shift our gaze to the western portion of this constellation, near its border with Andromeda, to check out M34, a mid-5th-magnitude open cluster containing about 100 stars.

Sitting 5.2° west-northwest of 2nd-magnitude Algol (Beta [β] Persei), M34 spans about half a degree, roughly the size of the Full Moon. In physical space, astronomers believe the group spans about 14 light-years and sits 1,400 light-years away. It’s best seen under lower magnifications, such as in binoculars or small amateur scopes (4 inches or so). You’ll spot several dozen stars brighter than 12th magnitude, with its brightest suns spread throughout the cluster.

Sunrise: 6:42 A.M. Sunset: 4:46 P.M. Moonrise: 10:08 A.M. Moonset: 6:57 P.M. Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (14%)

Friday, November 13The Moon reaches apogee, the farthest point from Earth in its orbit, at 12:50 P.M. EST. At that time, our satellite will be 252,040 miles (405,619 kilometers) from Earth.

Celebrate Friday the 13th with something spooky: a ghost in the constellation Andromeda. This evening, point your telescope toward 2nd-magnitude Mirach (Beta [β] Andromedae), already nearly 60° high in the east by 7 P.M. local time. One of the Princess’ brightest stars, Mirach is a cool, reddish M-type giant. It lies some 200 light-years away and shines nearly 2,000 times as brightly as our Sun.

But Mirach is not quite our target — we’re looking for its so-called ghost, just 6.8’ northwest of the star. You’ll need a big scope to see it, but look carefully: Can you spot a faint smudge of light, about 4’ across, close to the star? This is the Ghost of Mirach, a far more distant elliptical galaxy glowing at 10th magnitude and cataloged as NGC 404. It lies some 8 million to 10 million light-years away, just beyond the gravitational bounds of our Local Group of galaxies. It’s called a ghost because it appears almost like a ghostly image of the bright star Mirach, which dominates the view.

Sunrise: 6:43 A.M. Sunset: 4:45 P.M. Moonrise: 10:54 A.M. Moonset: 7:55 P.M. Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (21%)

Alison Klesman is senior editor of Astronomy magazine. She holds a Ph.D. in astronomy and has studied a variety of topics, from minor planets to supermassive black holes.

#6355. North America’s oldest footprints tell a story of drought and survival

Ancient footprints at White Sands reveal how people returned for nearly 2,000 years as drought and warming transformed an ice age lake.

The last ice age can sound like a time when landscapes barely changed across generations. But ancient footprints at White Sands tell a different story.

At White Sands in New Mexico, the footprint makers watched a lake shrink into a flat, salty mudflat called a playa, and a pine forest give way to sagebrush.

A severe drought came and went within about a century. Through it all, people kept walking the same shoreline for nearly 2,000 years.

A team led by Kathleen Springer and Jeffrey Pigati of the U.S. Geological Survey dug a new trench at the footprint site. Jessica Tierney of the University of Arizona reconstructed the climate from its mud.

The layers at White Sands National Park record conditions in steps of about 50 years, roughly a human generation.

“Even though these footprints have been buried in the gypsum mud for more than 20,000 years, they look like someone walked out on the playa yesterday,” Tierney said.

“This is an incredibly rare opportunity to be able to do paleoclimate reconstruction and combine it with archeology in the same exact place.”

The original trench, dug in 2020, was 36 feet (11 meters) long. The team extended it to 82 feet (25 meters), and the number of footprint layers rose from seven to 20.

Most of the measured footprints were consistent with children’s feet.

Of the 152 measured footprints, 72 were consistent with children around six years old, and another 12 with children around 12.

Eight came from toddlers under four, and 60 from adolescents or adults.

Mammoths, ground sloths, members of the dog family and possibly bears left tracks in the same layers, beside drag marks from people hauling loads on poles.

There was no sign of a camp, so the team read the site as a place people passed through rather than settled.

The first dates for the White Sands footprints, published in 2021, came from seeds of a water plant from the lake.

Critics argued those seeds could have absorbed old carbon from the lake water and so look older than they are.

Pine pollen doesn’t have that problem, because the trees took their carbon from the air.

Earlier pollen dates had carried uncertainties of more than 2,000 years, so they couldn’t settle the question.

The USGS lab sorted up to 75,000 pollen grains out of each sample with a cell-sorting machine and measured how much modern carbon the laboratory process introduced.

The uncertainty on each pollen date dropped fivefold.

The pollen dates came out younger than seed dates from the same layers, by up to 1,330 radiocarbon years.

The corrected dates placed the footprints between 23,500 and 21,700 years ago.

The oldest mud in the trench formed under standing water between about 24,200 and 23,600 years ago.

Lake Otero covered the site, and pine, fir and spruce made up 40% of the pollen blown in from the mountains.

The team estimated air temperature from microbial fats in the mud, whose makeup changes with temperature: about 54°F (12°C), roughly 7°F (4°C) colder than the area today.

Then the lake began to shrink. From about 23,600 years ago the sediment switched from lake clay to silt and sand washed in over land, and oak and sagebrush replaced the conifer forest.

Warming sped up around 22,400 years ago, and the upper layers filled with gypsum and salt left behind by evaporation.

The White Sands warming was the opposite of the trend across the rest of the Northern Hemisphere, which kept cooling until about 18,000 years ago.

Ocean records off California show the same early warming, which the authors suggested may have been widespread across the Southwest.

Between 24,200 and 23,600 years ago the basin was wet, and hydrogen in preserved leaf wax points to winter rain off the Pacific rather than summer monsoon rain.

Then, 23,200 years ago, a severe but short drought hit.

The water turned saltier, drought-tolerant piñon and juniper spread, and the shallow lake turned permanently into a mudflat wet only in patches.

The oldest footprint layer dates to that drought, when newly exposed ground became walkable.

The same moment shows up in Greenland ice cores as a sudden warming, one of a series of abrupt climate swings during the ice age.

The White Sands footprint dates carry smaller errors than the ice core’s, so the authors wrote that their record may date that event more sharply.

“This tells us that local changes in aridity at White Sands were quite large and followed global climate shifts,” Tierney said.

Another wet spell around 22,700 years ago left clay from a short-lived pond, and the water plant’s share of the pollen rose to 60% in some wet layers.

People kept walking the shoreline through every swing. The authors read that as a sign of how much the waning lake still offered.

Springer said early humans in the region “were real-time witnesses to a rapidly changing environment discernible within a human lifetime – that is really food for thought.”

Ed Jolie, a curator at the Arizona State Museum who is Oglala Lakota and Hodulgee Muscogee, noted that the findings “humanize the deep Indigenous past of the Americas.”

He said they support Native nations’ oral traditions of having been here since time immemorial.

The footprint counts are rough. Some excavated patches are small and crowded, so the team cautioned that its estimates of how many people walked each layer can’t be used for population figures.

Ages from foot length are approximations too. A larger question concerns the connection between Greenland’s warming and drought at White Sands.

Tierney and her colleagues don’t yet know why a warming spike over Greenland would dry out a valley in New Mexico. Working out that mechanism is their next step.

The 50-year resolution of the White Sands record gives them something to test ideas against.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#6354. Earwax’s surprisingly slippery but sticky properties deters insects

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Earwax is anything but waxy and may help protect the ear against insect intrusions

This fire ant is struggling to walk on a clump of earwax, a substance that experts think may exist in part to help keep our ears free of insects.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

There are few things more annoying than having a bug fly into your ear. But the body is prepared to fend off these insect invasions, says David Hu, a bioengineer at Georgia Tech.

The goop inside our ears may act as a natural insect repellent, Hu’s team reports 28 October in Soft Matter. What we call earwax is not really waxy at all. Instead, the brownish substance absorbs water, a property that might help it regulate moisture in the ear and keep bugs out, the new analysis shows. “[This] familiar biological material may represent a sophisticated physical defense against small arthropods,” says Stanislav Gorb, a functional morphologist at the University of Kiel in Germany, who was not involved with the work.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have not studied earwax as much as other body fluids, such as snot, spit or even pee. “It’s a big mystery why we even have [it] in our ears,” Hu says. It can frankly seem like a nuisance. Earwax can build up, clogging earbuds and hearing aids and interfering with hearing, so understanding this substance better may help resolve those problems.

Hu and colleagues analyzed the mechanical and chemical properties of 36 earwax samples from pigs, sheep, dogs, cows, rabbits and humans. They also observed how fire ants (Solenopsis invicta) reacted to both natural and synthetic earwax.

Even though ants seem able to scale kitchen cabinets with ease to invade countertops, they flounder when they attempt to climb earwax. Hu thinks the earwax sucks moisture from the ants’ feet that helps them grip. But earwax also sticks to ants’ bodies, causing the insects to start grooming incessantly trying to get rid of it. “It’s both sticky and slippery,” Hu says.

The chemical analyses provide some clues about the origins of these properties. Dead skin cells make up 60 percent of earwax, along with a smattering of oils and moisture. The earwax contains pores that Hu believes may be shaped like ink bottles to help it absorb twice its weight in water and prevent water from sloshing around in the ear canal. Like snot, earwax has a huge range of consistencies.

Under normal conditions, earwax becomes dry and crumbly in about 10 weeks. As it dries, it’s moved outward by a layer of cells lining the ear canal that act as a cleaning conveyor belt. In this way, the ear maintains just the right thickness of earwax to keep insects at bay, Hu says. “It’s most potent when it’s thin,” he explains. “Too much, and the ants can use their tiny claws to grab hold and climb in.”

Hu admits there’s no practical way to turn earwax into a commercial insect repellent. Each person has a volume of earwax about equivalent to that of a grain of rice in each ear at any given time, says Hu, so even if you add up all the earwax on Earth, “it’s a pretty rare substance.” But, he adds, companies “are trying to come up with biodegradable and biofriendly ways to deal with insects.” And, says Gorb, perhaps earwax “could inspire a new generation of physical, nontoxic pest control surfaces,” that could provide coatings for protecting stored food, agricultural products and technology.

#6353. Monkeys that lived through a deadly outbreak showed surprising caution around food

Japanese macaques from groups hit by a deadly outbreak were more likely to avoid food on feces, even if they had never tested positive.

In the first weeks of COVID-19, many households wiped down their groceries before putting them away.

Japanese macaques that lived through a deadly outbreak of their own also showed greater caution around food.

Macaques from groups where the virus had spread refused food placed on a soiled surface far more often than those from a group it never reached.

And the virus they had survived isn’t even known to spread through food.

Stephan Kaufhold and Federico Rossano of the University of California San Diego‘s Department of Cognitive Science ran the tests at a primate sanctuary in southern Texas.

The researchers tested whether monkeys would eat a grape placed on feces.

The experiment measured food avoidance, which does not necessarily indicate disgust.

The sanctuary’s Japanese macaques descend from a troop moved from Japan to Texas in 1972. Today they live in four separate fenced enclosures.

In January 2020, the sanctuary confirmed that a virus called simian retrovirus Type II was circulating in the Japanese macaques.

A long-tailed macaque that had retired from a research laboratory had carried it in without showing symptoms.

Late in 2019, the virus had likely changed enough to spread to the Japanese macaques.

Some infected monkeys died quickly of severe bleeding.

Others carried it with no symptoms, and some later lost weight and fell ill with other infections, much as people with AIDS do.

The virus passes through blood and saliva, mostly in bites and scratches during fights, and it has never been shown to spread through feces or food.

Three of the four groups went through the outbreak. The fourth, called Kyoto, didn’t.

Between October 2022 and March 2024, the team set two baited objects on the ground inside each enclosure and filmed what happened.

One was a plain piece of wood. The other was real macaque feces, collected from healthy animals and sealed under clear epoxy so it looked fresh but had no smell and couldn’t infect anyone.

A grape was placed on each object, and every monkey was free to take both.

Monkeys from the three outbreak groups ate the grape off the feces in 47% of 117 trials. Monkeys from Kyoto ate it in 79% of 80 trials.

So a monkey that had lived through the outbreak usually took the clean grape and left the other one lying there. A monkey from Kyoto usually ate both.

Within the outbreak groups, some monkeys had tested positive for the virus and some never had.

Kaufhold’s team compared the two, and the uninfected monkeys avoided the dirty grape about as much as the infected ones did. Both avoided it far more than the Kyoto monkeys.

In an interview with Earth.com, Kaufhold said that was the result he hadn’t expected.

“What surprised us was that animals within the exposed groups that had not been infected avoided the contaminated food just as much as those that had,” he said.

Kaufhold said the team doesn’t know why some monkeys escaped infection. Their immune systems may have resisted it, or they may have stayed out of the fights that spread it.

“Either way, the shift in behavior seems to follow having lived through the outbreak, for example witnessing others getting sick and dying, rather than being infected oneself,” he told Earth.com.

Only nine monkeys in the outbreak groups are confirmed uninfected, and the team treats that comparison as preliminary.

The outbreak groups showed greater caution around feces, even though the virus is not known to spread that way.

Kaufhold said the pattern “suggests a general increase in pathogen sensitivity rather than avoidance of the specific transmission route.”

In another experiment in the same paper, the team tested macaques from seven species, one at a time, with a sliding table that held the same two objects.

Among those tested, 14 were born at the sanctuary and raised by their mothers, while 15 were former pets raised by people.

The former pets had about twice the odds of taking food off the feces that the sanctuary-born monkeys did, even after years of living in monkey groups.

Kaufhold told Earth.com that one possibility is that the former pets “missed the chance to learn these behaviors from their mothers and other macaques early in life.”

Earlier studies found that young macaques watch their mothers and older groupmates forage, and that what they see others do shapes what they eat.

There is a cost, Kaufhold said. “Pathogen avoidance is always a trade-off.”

“Being too sensitive means leaving resources like food on the table, while being too indiscriminate increases exposure to pathogens and potentially disease.”

The outbreak monkeys were paying that cost in grapes.

The researchers can’t rule out that the four groups already differed before the outbreak, because nobody tested them then.

They also can’t yet say whether each monkey learned the caution on its own or picked it up from the group.

One precedent they cite is a troop of wild baboons in Kenya. A tuberculosis outbreak in the 1980s killed the troop’s most aggressive males, and the calmer culture that followed was passed on to males who joined years later.

Kaufhold said two questions come next: how long the heightened caution lasts, and whether monkeys that join these groups later pick it up.

“If newcomers picked up the increased caution, that would suggest social transmission, which could lead to a group-specific tradition,” he said.

Kaufhold said the macaque data “does not directly speak to how human behavior changed during and after COVID-19, but there are some interesting parallels.”

Studies of people found that disgust sensitivity rose during the pandemic, including toward things that had nothing to do with how the coronavirus spread.

The authors argue that human disgust was built on an older system for avoiding disease, one that changes with experience.

The team hasn’t yet measured whether that caution will still be there in the Texas enclosures a few years from now. They hope to go back and find out.

The full study was published in the journal Royal Society Open Science.

#6352. Where children live may influence how well they focus

Children in greener neighborhoods scored slightly higher on attention tests, suggesting nearby trees and parks may play a role in focus.

Children often do better on attention tasks after a walk in the park or time in a school garden.

But researchers have had mixed answers about whether living near trees and parks is also linked to better focus.

A large study of American children now finds a small connection between neighborhood greenery and attention.

Links with reading and vocabulary were less clear after researchers accounted for family income.

Carina Fowler led the study at Washington University in St. Louis. She is a postdoctoral researcher in the lab of Deanna Barch, a professor in the Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences.

“If a child lives closer to green space, and has more access to green space, does this help them pay attention on demand when it’s required, and do they do better at school on achievement tests?” Fowler said.

The researchers explored an idea called attention restoration theory. It suggests that nature gives the mind a break from the effort of staying focused.

The theory describes two kinds of attention: one we use to concentrate on a task, and another that responds automatically to things around us.

Phones, TVs and traffic can grab that automatic attention completely, while trees and parks may hold it gently enough to let the mind wander.

This may give our ability to concentrate a chance to recover.

Fowler said earlier research suggests people dislike having nothing to see or hear, or sitting alone with their thoughts in a quiet room.

“It seems people need something to be occupying them a little bit – but not too much – and that nature can provide that really well,” Fowler said.

The team used data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study, which recruited children near 21 sites across the continental United States.

The analysis included 11,868 children who joined between 2016 and 2018, aged nine or 10.

For each child’s home, the team studied the surrounding census tract, an area used in the national census that is roughly the size of a neighborhood.

Satellite images showed how much land trees covered.

Records checked by the Trust for Public Land showed how much land was parkland. The researchers averaged the tree and park percentages to give each child a green space score.

Across the group, the combined score averaged about 11%.

The children took five short tests that involved remembering things, switching between rules, ignoring distractions and processing information quickly.

The team combined the results into an attention score.

The score used a scale similar to an IQ test, with 100 in the middle and a typical spread of about 15 points.

Reading and vocabulary tests produced a second score that gave a rough picture of school skills.

The team looked at each child at one point in time. That means the results can show a connection, but cannot prove that greenery caused higher scores.

Children’s focus depends on many things. The researchers considered sex and how well off each neighborhood was.

They also included ADHD, stimulant medicines, sleep problems, weekly screen time and tobacco exposure before birth.

Other checks covered air pollution, physical activity and whether children felt safe from crime in their neighborhood.

According to the authors, no earlier study of green space and attention had included children’s own sense of safety.

“You have to feel safe in the green space to have an effect,” Fowler said.

After those checks, a 10-percentage-point increase in green space was linked to an attention score 0.76 points higher. Reading and vocabulary scores were 0.83 points higher.

A 10-percentage-point rise would mean going from 10% to 20%, for example.

The score differences were small: less than one point on a scale with a typical spread of 15 points.

Many children had little greenery nearby. About half lived in areas with a green space score below 10%, and about one in 10 had a score below 1%.

The authors suggested that even a small increase in greenery might matter in those places. Attention and school skills at this age can help predict later health, earnings and education.

Greener neighborhoods tend to have cleaner air, and studies have linked air pollution to attention problems. The team checked whether tiny pollution particles could explain some of the results.

These particles measure no more than about one ten-thousandth of an inch across, or 2.5 micrometers.

Lower particle pollution explained a small part of the link with both scores, which surprised the authors because they had expected it to explain none.

“There is something to the idea that air quality is partially explaining why green space is helping our attention,” Fowler said.

Exercise did not explain the link. Children in greener areas did not report more days with at least an hour of activity, although more active children scored higher on both measures.

The team then added family income to the analysis, which already included how well off the neighborhood was.

The link between greenery and attention became about half as large, but it remained.

The link with reading and vocabulary was no longer statistically significant. This makes it harder to tell how much greenery itself might matter for those skills.

The authors offered two possible explanations. Green space may have a weaker link with school skills, or it may help focus sooner while any effect on learning takes years to build.

The attention score combined several skills, so it was not a test of attention alone.

The school skills score covered reading and vocabulary, leaving out math, science and writing.

The study also included relatively few rural children because most of its brain-imaging centers are in cities.

And the team measured greenery at only one point in each child’s life, so it could not show what happens after a move to a greener area.

The authors suggested testing whether greener school grounds help children learn.

They also raised the possibility that keeping children inside during recess as punishment for poor focus or grades could make those problems worse.

Both ideas need testing, as does whether planting trees near homes or schools improves attention.

Experiments and studies that follow children over many years could help answer those questions.

The study is published in the journal Environment International.
