Madi Allen was 12 years old when she almost died from flu. Now 28, she shared her story with Live Science.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In February 2011, Madi Allen, a healthy 12-year-old in Central Illinois, who loved playing sports, almost died from the flu. The influenza B virus resulted in her developing necrotizing pneumonia, where the infection triggers inflammation that destroys the tissue of the lungs, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), and her kidneys shut down. She was put on life support and dialysis, and was intubated for five weeks. She spent another two months in hospital and a decade recovering from the damage caused.

Allen, now 28, shared her experience with Live Science.

I was 12 years old when it all started. I was just a normal seventh grader, I played soccer and basketball. I didn't really have any health issues beforehand — just sports-induced asthma.

That weekend, I started to feel a little sick, but nothing too bad. My mom kept giving me over-the-counter medicine and it would work for a bit, then once it wore off, it would get really bad. I'd planned to go to one of my friend's birthday parties then spend the night with my best friend. I went to the party, but I texted my mom saying I should come home because I really wasn't feeling well, which was not usual for me at all. That night I asked my mom to sleep with me because I just felt terrible.

That was Saturday. By Sunday night, the only position that I could get comfortable in was my mom holding me like a baby. My mom just held me all weekend. My whole body just hurt and I started feeling like I couldn't breathe properly. That got way worse Monday morning.

We were waiting for my pediatrician to open up and my mom suggested taking a shower, saying, "Maybe that will help you feel a bit better before we go to the doctor." She had to help me take a shower because I was so weak, I couldn't stand by myself. She stepped away for a second just to grab a towel and said that when she came back, my lips were turning gray and my eyes were starting to look sunken in. She knew that something was not right so she called my dad, who was at the grocery store, and told him to just leave everything, that we need to get to the hospital.

Allen was put on life support and had to be intubated for five weeks after getting sick with flu.

Our local hospital is just a small rural hospital — everybody gets transferred out. They diagnosed me with double pneumonia and then sent me to a different hospital 30 minutes away that specialized more in kids.

My dad rode with me in the ambulance while my mom went home and grabbed a few things — she thought we'd just be there for a few days. By the time we got to the second hospital, I was in respiratory distress. They wanted to intubate me straight away but were waiting until my mom got there so she could talk to me — my dad did the best he could, but my dad didn't know how to calm me down.

I don't think the doctors even told me that they were putting me to sleep. My mom had to be the one to tell me. I remember being very scared. They put this mask on my face for the BiPAP [bilevel positive airway pressure machine, which delivers pressurized air to a patient] and I felt like that was suffocating me. It didn't feel like it was helping at all, which, I guess, at that point, it wasn't. They were just trying everything they could. I was begging them to take it off of me, crying and just saying, "one minute, just take it off for one minute."

Finally my mom tried to calm me down and she's like, "They're gonna have to put you to sleep now." I remember her telling me, "You're just gonna go to sleep for like a couple of hours and then you're gonna wake up and you're gonna feel a lot better."

My mom had to leave the room while they were doing that. As she was walking out the door, the last thing I said was "Mom" and then I put my hands in a heart shape. That was the last thing I did and the last time my mom heard my voice for five weeks.

After I was intubated, things got worse. I had to be put on life support so needed to be moved to a bigger hospital in St. Louis, Missouri. The flight team came to evaluate me and they later told me they didn't think they were ever going to get me to Saint Louis. They thought I wasn't going to make the trip. But they said my mom was begging them to help me, everyone in my family was begging them, so they did everything they could to get me on the helicopter. They worked on me for several hours — every time they tried to move me something would go wrong — but eventually they got me there.

The doctors had to call my parents to get permission to do surgery and put me on life support. My mom said that every time she heard my dad's phone ring, she thought they were calling to tell them that I didn't make it. They were told twice that it was more than likely I was going to pass than make it. They were trying to prepare my parents that I wasn't going to make it.

After getting out of hospital, it took years for Allen to recover, eventually having part of her lung removed that had been badly damaged by the virus.

I woke up five weeks later, and it was very confusing. Everybody was told if I asked what day it was, just to tell me the day of the week. When someone accidentally told me the date, I started crying because my aunt was supposed to be getting married a few weeks later and I was worried about being at her wedding. My mom wasn't there, so my dad had to calm me down and then he told me the wedding had been pushed to October so I could be there.

The second thing I was worried about was that I was supposed to take a test on the Constitution and that I'd missed it. I ended up taking it in the hospital. I was there for 93 days. I got out the very last week of school, so I got to go in on the last day of school and surprise my classmates and my teachers.

That summer, I didn't really do anything besides go to doctor's appointments. I was doing physical therapy, occupational therapy and speech therapy — literally all my time was spent at the hospital in therapy. I'd missed three months of school, but I got to start eighth grade with all my friends, and I ended up playing basketball again. But the next several years was a lot of hard work of trying to get back to my normal.

It probably took the rest of junior high and high school to get back to how I would have been before. It was a very long process and during that time I got sick a lot, so I ended up back in the hospital several times. And it was hard going through that as a teenager — I felt like everybody else is living their normal life, and I felt like I missed out on a lot. Looking back now, I still feel like I did miss out a lot. But I think we made the best of the circumstances.

During COVID, when I was 22, I kept getting sick, and the doctors finally told me that part of my lung was so damaged from the flu it was causing infections, so they gave me an option of getting part of my lung removed. It was a major surgery, but I did it and that was probably the best decision I ever made, because it's been five years and I have not been in the hospital once.

I moved to Florida about three years ago, and I started working as a medical assistant in a pulmonary clinic. This semester I got accepted into respiratory therapy school, so for the next two years, I'm going to be in school for respiratory therapy. It's kind of a full circle moment, to come back into the medical field, because there was a point in my life where everybody was asking me, "Oh, do you want to be a doctor? Do you want to be a nurse?" And I'm like, "Absolutely not." I was still so sick that I was there all the time. I never wanted to be there.

I went to college and I got a degree in criminal justice, but I never really knew what I wanted to do. I ended up getting a job at our local hospital — that first hospital that I went to. Every time they put me in the ER I just loved being there. That job made me realize that this is what I wanted to do.

When people hear my story, they don't realize that if I don't tell the end — after the hospital until now — they don't realize that my life didn't go back to normal after. It's taken 10 years. And it's hard. Some of the other family members that we've gotten to know through Families Fighting Flu, it's difficult listening to their stories. Sometimes I feel like I have this survivor's guilt. Their stories sound exactly like mine — but their kids didn't make it.

Before I got sick I got the flu shot every year, but that year we just got busy and it got put on the back burner. Since getting sick I have always made it a priority to get the flu shot every year. I know it is not a guarantee that I will never get the flu again — but hopefully it will reduce the chances of it ever getting that bad again.

With thanks to Families Fighting Flu, a non-profit organization that promotes flu vaccination and raises awareness of the severity of the infectious disease through families that have been affected.

#6349. Time between pregnancies may shape how fast mothers age

Each pregnancy adds biological age that takes months to come off, and birth spacing may decide how much a mother recovers before the next one.

Tests suggest that biological age rises during pregnancy and falls again in the months after birth. Researchers are now asking whether the time between pregnancies affects how fully those changes reverse.

Two Harvard researchers propose that the time a woman gets between pregnancies, not only how many she has, may shape how fast she ages for decades.

If the next pregnancy begins before that recovery is finished, the extra age may not be fully reversed, the authors wrote. The effect could then build with each closely spaced birth.

Stephen Albright and Jesse Poganik of Harvard Medical School and Brigham and Women’s Hospital laid out the idea in a review article. It pulls together studies from Europe, the United States, Israel and the Philippines.

The result is a hypothesis with testable predictions attached, not a new trial, and Poganik said the changes it describes don’t necessarily amount to damage.

“Our previous research has found that biological age transiently rises during pregnancy, peaking around the third trimester or at the time of delivery,” said Poganik, the corresponding author.

“If we accept the idea that these short-term changes in biological age occur, the question is how we can relate those changes to the overall trajectory of aging over the course of a lifetime.”

Biological age is an estimate of how much age-related change a body’s cells and tissues have accumulated, separate from the years on a birth certificate.

One way to estimate it is to read chemical tags on DNA that shift in a predictable pattern as people get older. Researchers call those readouts epigenetic clocks.

Run those clocks on blood drawn through a pregnancy and the number climbs as the pregnancy goes on, then partly falls after the birth.

Women on three continents show the same pattern, and so do mice. The authors wrote that this level of agreement is uncommon in their field.

The changes behind the number are physical. Blood volume rises by about half.

Cortisol, a stress hormone, climbs through pregnancy, and estrogen runs at roughly 100 times its usual level. The body also builds a new organ, the placenta, from nothing.

A detailed picture of the recovery comes from Israel, where researchers analyzed 76 routine lab tests from more than 300,000 pregnancies.

About half of those markers needed anywhere from three months to a year to return to where they had been before the pregnancy.

An aging clock built from those same lab results showed a dip before a large rise. In the first trimester a woman’s results looked about five years younger than her age.

From there they rose by about 20 years toward delivery, and it took roughly a year for them to recover.

Not every system recovers on the same schedule. Among more than 200,000 people, the reading from a clock built from wearable pulse sensors rose by about 3.5 years during pregnancy, then declined only slowly after birth.

Brain scans of first-time mothers showed gray matter volume falling across nearly all of the cortex during pregnancy and only partly recovering afterward.

The most direct evidence comes from a 2026 study that followed 130 women from pregnancy through nearly four years after the birth.

Among women who became pregnant again, the decline in their measured pace of aging was interrupted, and two other aging measures moved in the same direction.

Albright and Poganik call the time between a birth and the next conception the recovery window, and their hypothesis is simple to state.

Each pregnancy adds some biological age, and given enough time the body can undo at least part of it.

Under their hypothesis, another pregnancy could add to any biological-age increase that has not yet reversed.

Two women with the same number of children could therefore end up aging at different rates, depending on how far apart the births were.

The authors wrote that this is their central prediction, and it hasn’t been directly tested. No study has yet measured the spacing of pregnancies alongside biological age tracked for decades afterward.

Mothers of many children tend to die earlier in some populations and not in others, and the reasons remain unclear.

In the Finnish Twin Cohort, the risk of dying was highest among women with no births and women with five or more, and lowest among women with two or three.

Among adoptive parents, death rates declined as the number of adopted children increased.

A study of 2,356 women aged 35 to 74 linked more births to small increases in epigenetic age, measured well after their last pregnancy.

In 1,735 young women in the Philippines, with an average age of about 22, each additional pregnancy was linked to roughly two to three months of extra aging.

Spacing could explain why the count alone gives such mixed results, the authors wrote. Where women with many children tend to space them well, the count would carry little cost.

“It’s possible that this could change the overall trajectory of aging,” Poganik said.

“We know that some level of parity, or carrying a pregnancy to term, is actually beneficial to a person’s lifespan.”

The World Health Organization has recommended since 2005 that women wait at least 24 months after a live birth before conceiving again.

The advice rests on evidence linking short gaps to more preterm and low-weight births.

One review of 129 studies and nearly 47 million pregnancies linked gaps of 18 to 23 months to the best outcomes for babies. Gaps under six months were most consistently linked to harm for both baby and mother.

When a new pregnancy began six months after a birth, instead of 18 months, only women 35 and older faced a substantially higher chance of dying or becoming severely ill.

The age pattern fits their idea, Albright and Poganik wrote, because an older mother starts the recovery period biologically older, with less reserve.

Some factors were associated with differences in recovery.

Among about 120 women in one cohort, those who breastfed exclusively had a lower biological age three months after birth, whatever their body mass index.

A higher body mass index before pregnancy predicted a higher biological age afterward.

Sleep loss and chronic stress are suspected of slowing recovery too, though the authors found little or no research on either after birth.

Not every population fits. Tsimane women, who farm and forage for a living, have many children and little spare food.

Over a 10-year study their nutrition and immune markers largely held up however many children they had.

But those measures weren’t combined into a biological age, the authors wrote, so the cost they propose can’t be ruled out there.

Whether the extra age is wear, or the body remodeling itself for a demanding job, isn’t settled either. Clocks designed to tell the two apart are one way to find out.

Poganik said the work has a nearer-term purpose as well.

“What motivates me on a more near-term basis is addressing current clinical challenges, including the huge maternal mortality crisis in the United States compared with other industrialized countries,” he said.

“Any insights we can gain that can improve the health of mothers makes this a worthwhile research endeavor.”

The question underneath all of it is whether an incomplete recovery leaves a mother permanently older on the clocks, or whether the deficit fades given enough time.

Answering it means measuring biological age through several pregnancies, then following those women for 10 to 20 years, and no cohort has done that.

Until then, the 24-month guidance rests on pregnancy outcomes. Poganik said any advice based on a mother’s biological age would have to wait for that longer follow-up.

The review was published in the journal Trends in Endocrinology & Metabolism.

#6348. Little Ice Age cooling in Europe may have raised the risk of rickets

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Skeletal remains with signs of vitamin D deficiencies hint at how climate change impacted health

A volcano-fueled chilly climate during the 18th and 19th centuries may have made winter in England so bad, as depicted in this 19th century painting of a man collecting wood, that it raised the risk of kids getting rickets, a condition caused by vitamin D deficiency.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

England isn’t renowned for its weather. But just a few centuries ago, climate change–fueled conditions may have been so bad that they put children’s health at risk.

Calcium mineralization in the teeth and skeletons of people who lived in rural northern England suggests that children growing up during the height of the Little Ice Age routinely developed vitamin D deficiencies, researchers report November 5 in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology. In the worst cases, these deficiencies developed into rickets, a bone disorder that can occur when people don’t get enough ultraviolet light.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Previous skeletal studies suggest that rickets became more common among Europeans during the 18th and 19th centuries. One culprit may have been the Industrial Revolution, when many Europeans lived in UV-poor polluted cities and often worked indoors. The unusually cold climate may have added “an extra layer of difficulty” to getting enough sunlight, says Ellen Kendall, a bioarcheologist at Durham University in England

The Little Ice Age was a period of global cooling from the 13th to 19th centuries caused by extreme solar cycles and a series of volcanic eruptions, which can cool the planet by ejecting aerosols into the atmosphere that block sunlight. In the last 200 years of the era, 18 major eruptions helped spur a temperature drop of 2 to 3 degrees Celsius over northern Europe.

Kendall and colleagues wondered how this cold climate affected health. They examined calcium deposition — how the essential mineral is incorporated into bones — in the remains of 21 people buried from 1711 to 1829 in the town of North Shields. Calcium often doesn’t fully mineralize in people with vitamin D delicacies, leaving voids in teeth as they grow.

The team found bands of failed calcium mineralization in the teeth, suggesting seasonal spates of vitamin D deficiencies. Some skeletons also showed signs of rickets. North Shields was a small rural town that hadn’t yet undergone industrialization, so these deficiencies probably weren’t due to bad air conditions.

The unusually cold weather may have changed people’s behavior during the winter, Kendall says. Residents may have kept their kids indoors or bundled them up so that little skin was exposed when they did go outside, preventing them from getting enough UV light, she says.

However, climate was still just one factor among many — including gender roles, diet and pollution — that shaped vitamin D deficiencies at the time, says Kendall. “Humans are very messy to study,” she says. “That’s one of the things that makes them so very fascinating.”

#6347. A tiny plant’s unusual sex life depends on water flowing uphill

Common liverworts carry water up their stalks without a pump, helping sperm reach elevated eggs and revealing how the plants evolved.

Water runs downhill, and that’s a problem for liverworts, small plants whose sperm can reach an egg only by swimming.

In the common liverwort, a flat green species, the female holds her eggs up on a short stalk, away from the damp ground.

A new study found that the outside of that stalk carries water upward, against gravity, to the eggs at the top.

The upward flow helps resolve a conflict between fertilization and spore dispersal.

Height makes fertilization harder. But height also helps the plant spread its spores, and the study traces how the stalk came to handle both jobs.

Bo Xu, a professor at the Institute of Botany of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, led the work, and Xiaotong Qi is the study’s first author.

The team studied Marchantia polymorpha, the best-studied liverwort in biology labs.

Liverworts, mosses and hornworts belong to a group called bryophytes. They make no flowers or seeds, and they don’t have true roots.

They also lack the complex network of water-carrying tissue that larger plants rely on.

In bryophytes, a sperm cell has to travel through water to reach an egg.

Once an egg is fertilized, it grows into an embryo. The embryo then becomes a structure that makes spores, and those spores spread out and grow into new plants.

Every bryophyte has to meet both needs at once. Fertilization depends on water, while spores spread better from a higher, drier spot.

How small plants managed that is part of the larger story of how plants colonized land.

On a female common liverwort, a stalk lifts the egg-holding organs above the ground.

Xu’s team found that the stalk and the head on top of it carry water upward along their outer surface.

The flow depends on several kinds of tiny structures, each placed in a precise position relative to the others.

The researchers used three-dimensional X-ray imaging to map how those structures fit together on the stalk.

Water moving up that surface helps sperm reach eggs held well above the wet ground.

Keeping those surface structures intact helped water-based fertilization succeed, the team found.

One protein, called MpLAS, controls how all of those surface structures develop. It belongs to a family of proteins called GRAS, which switch other genes on and off.

MpLAS works by guiding how cells divide as they grow.

A second GRAS protein, MpGRAS10, helps build the stalk itself. It boosts the activity of two genes, MpKAOL1 and MpKAOL2, which help the plant make compounds related to gibberellin.

In many plants, gibberellin is the hormone that makes stems grow longer.

So one protein helps raise the eggs, and another builds the surface that gets water up to them.

Xu’s team also compared the common liverwort with its relatives and worked backward through their family tree.

The female stalk appears to have evolved only once in this group of liverworts, and several later lineages lost it.

The stalk turned up before the surface structures that carry water.

The researchers read that order as two separate steps. The elevated stalk helped the spores produced after fertilization spread farther.

The surface network came later and dealt with that problem.

In their account, later traits may have arisen to make earlier ones work better, by fixing what those earlier traits couldn’t do.

They said competing demands like these can push a complex structure to evolve one piece at a time.

Comparisons among living liverworts suggest that the stalk evolved before its water-carrying surface structures.

That sequence supports the team’s proposed explanation, although it does not prove how those traits evolved.

The findings could also inspire engineers.

By carrying water upward without a pump, the liverwort offers a model for surfaces designed to move liquid on their own.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Plants.

#6346. The Sky Today on Friday, November 6: Nab the North America Nebula

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

As fall gets into full swing, we are seeing less of the summertime stars. By 6 P.M. local time, the Summer Triangle — which flies high overhead on short summer nights — is now starting to set in the west. Lowest of its three points is Vega in Lyra; to Vega’s upper left is Altair in Aquila, while Deneb in Cygnus is almost directly above Vega and the highest of the three.

With no Moon in the sky, let’s use Deneb to find a favorite deep-sky object: NGC 7000, the North America Nebula. It’s a great small scope target, and its location just 3° east of Deneb makes it easy to center in the eyepiece. However, this huge emission nebula stretches about 2° across, so note that it requires a larger field of view to capture all in one go. It definitely benefits from a nebula filter if you have one.

On the sky, the nebula’s western side looks like the eastern coast of the continent for which it is named, and vice versa. The curve that mimics the Gulf of Mexico is particularly prominent, so start there if you’re having trouble seeing the shape. Look also to NGC 7000’s west — across a dark gulf, you’ll see a fainter, more compact patch of nebulosity. This is IC 5067/5070, also known as the Pelican Nebula.

#6345. Major study argues we need immediate rules to protect young people from the harms of digital media

Lancet experts say digital media harms to young people come from app design and weak rules, not lack of willpower. They urge governments to act now.

When teenagers can’t stop scrolling on their mobile devices, the easiest explanation is to label them as having weak self-control.

A group of public health experts has a different answer. The feed was built to keep that thumb moving, and the responsibility belongs to the companies that built it and the governments that let them.

In a three-paper Series in The Lancet, the experts said the harm that digital media does to young people comes from business models, design choices and weak rules. They want governments to act now, before anyone has proof of cause and effect.

If they’re right, the question is no longer how many hours a child spends on a screen. It is what the apps on that screen were designed to do.

Professor Ilona Kickbusch of the Digital Transformations for Health Lab in Switzerland chaired the Series. Dr. Jay Shaw of the University of Toronto led its first paper.

The caveat arrives early. Heavy, addiction-like use is linked to poorer mental health, sleep and physical activity, Kickbusch said, but the evidence isn’t conclusive. A link isn’t proof of cause, and the authors rate the evidence low in certainty.

In an interview with Earth.com, she said the size of the effects is only half the question. “If you consider how many children are now using digital media, even small adverse effects might have significant public health consequences,” she said.

“That is why we are calling for a precautionary approach to policy rather than reacting only after harm has occurred.”

Open almost any social app and the feed never ends. Designers built that bottomless scroll deliberately, Shaw and his co-authors wrote, and it has encouraged amounts of screen time already known to be harmful.

The companies behind those features have lobbied to hold off regulation while knowing about the harms, the authors wrote.

“Most digital platforms are designed by companies to capture attention and collect data, not to protect health,” Shaw said. He added that infinite scroll, autoplay and personalized recommendation feeds are deliberate design choices that draw attention.

Scale turns a design detail into a public health question. By one estimate the authors cite, people who were online in 2025 spent an average of 141 minutes a day on social media apps, about two hours and 20 minutes.

In a 2025 survey of more than 10,000 adults in the United States, the average was more than 6 hours a day on phone apps, which is most of a school day.

Shaw’s paper compares the technology industry with tobacco and ultra-processed food. Both of those industries worked to weaken regulation while their products harmed health.

Governments have allowed digital companies to regulate themselves for decades, the Series reports, and commercial growth has come before health.

“Technology companies are borrowing a playbook well known from tobacco and fossil fuels: manufacture doubt, discredit critics, frame regulation as a threat to freedom,” said Professor Barbara Prainsack of the University of Vienna, a co-author on the Series.

Missing regulation doesn’t mean a technology goes ungoverned, she added. It means the companies set the rules instead of public policy.

Shaw and his co-authors called today’s approaches to governing that system deeply insufficient to protect public health.

They also describe adolescence and early adulthood as periods when the brain and social life are especially sensitive. The idealized selves people build online are linked to body shaming and poorer mental health, especially in young people.

Asked by Earth.com what surprised her most in the evidence, Kickbusch named the gaps. “What was most surprising about the evidence on the health impacts of children’s digital media use was what it doesn’t tell us,” she said.

Most studies measure individual behavior, such as screen time, she explained. Researchers have paid very little attention to the bigger structures, such as content created by algorithms and targeted advertising.

Young people also care about the benefits of going online and about AI, she said, and researchers have studied both of these areas less.

Access to data is another problem. “The most valuable data on how these platforms actually affect users are hidden within technology companies, limiting independent scrutiny and slowing scientific progress,” said Louise Holly, a Series author at DTH-Lab.

Shaw’s paper lists eight recommendations for researchers. One is to audit and publish the practices of technology companies that harm health, using insider accounts from former employees and investigative reporting.

Another is to keep industry money out of the research itself, a lesson the authors take from tobacco and pharmaceuticals.

Single measures such as age limits aren’t enough on their own, so the Series calls for action at the company, national and global levels at once.

Companies would have to test new products and features for harm before releasing them. They would also share data on how those features affect users’ health with vetted public-interest researchers.

A global treaty through the World Health Organization would set baseline standards, so weak rules in one country can’t undo progress elsewhere. A dedicated international body would monitor AI harms to children and young people.

Kickbusch told Earth.com that governments must work on several fronts in parallel: reduce access, regulate individual technologies and address the commercial models and algorithms behind social media. They also need to cooperate across borders, she said. “They must accept this is a major public health issue!”

Lawsuits are part of the picture too. Courts can compel companies to disclose internal documents in a way regulators often can’t, Kickbusch said. She sees litigation as one route to accountability among several, not a substitute for regulation.

The authors also worked with a youth advisory group of six adults aged 23 to 30, who talked with them about the lived experience the research can’t capture.

The steps governments and companies need to take will take time, Kickbusch said, because they are politically contested. Families don’t have to wait.

“Meanwhile, parents must help children mitigate risks by significantly reducing their use of digital media and the access to smartphones. They must explain to children how digital platforms and algorithms work,” she said.

Families who understand the design features and the commercial motives behind the platforms can protect themselves better, she explained, even when cutting back leads to difficult conversations at home.

“And parents themselves must change their social media use and be an example for their children,” she added.

No one has proved that the design features cause the harms linked to them, or measured how large those harms are, and the authors say so plainly. The links are modest in size and rest on evidence they rate as low in certainty.

The scope is also wider than the kids with phones. The same industries shape the health of people who don’t use the technology themselves, Shaw’s team wrote.

By the International Telecommunication Union‘s count, 2.2 billion people had no internet access in 2025. Africa was the least connected region.

Shaw said the field needs much more research into how specific design choices change the way people use digital media, instead of only measuring how long they spend online. That research depends on data the companies now keep to themselves.

Until that data is shared, the most important measurements of how these platforms affect adolescent health stay inside the companies that built them.

The full study was published in the journal The Lancet.

A new study points to testosterone and proteins in the skin as reasons why males and females experience temperatures differently.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's a common observation that women often prefer warmer temperatures and feel cold more easily than men do, and the same trend appears among females of other species. Now, a study offers new clues as to what drives this preference — and testosterone may play a part.

Skin carries sensors to detect heat and cold that influence each organism's decision to stay in or move out of an environment. The new study, published Oct. 28 in the Journal of Physiology, found that these sensors activate at higher temperatures in female mice, which appears to shift their preferred temperature roughly 7 degrees Fahrenheit (4 degrees Celsius) higher than that of male mice. Testosterone seems to influence this difference in activation.

"You could say it's just a cute observation of no particular importance," said study co-author Peter McNaughton, a pharmacologist at King's College London who studies pain, thermal sensation and thermoregulation. "[But] it's got practical ramifications," in that it might be important in designing buildings and spaces that accommodate people, he told Live Science.

Proteins in the skin's nerve endings activate in response to warmth or cold. "You can look at them like little electrical generators in the nerve endings," said Dr. Michael Caterina, a neuroscientist at Johns Hopkins University who was not involved in the research.

When activated, these proteins allow charged ions to enter sensory nerve cells, which, in turn, transmit electrical signals to the brain. The circuits a given nerve cell connects to determines our perception of heat or cold, Caterina told Live Science.

Beyond humans, it is known that many female animals, including mice and birds, prefer slightly warmer temperatures than their male counterparts do. So the researchers set up an experiment to investigate these differences.

They put 30 male and 27 female mice on two adjacent plates of different temperatures — one at 91.4 degrees Fahrenheit (33 degrees Celsius) and another that varied between lower and higher temperatures. A camera tracked the mice's movements and calculated how much time they spent on each plate.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Both male and female mice spent more time at the 91.4 F plate when the second plate was cooler. However, when put next to a plate measuring 100.4 F (38 C), female mice spent significantly more time on the warmer plate than male mice did. The average preferred surface temperature was approximately 89.6 F (32 C) for male mice and 96.8 F (36 C) for female mice.

"Since the top of the cage was completely open, there was no question of the air temperature affecting the mice," McNaughton said, so the preference was driven solely by the sensors in their skin. The researchers also measured the internal and skin temperatures of the mice and confirmed that there were no significant differences between the sexes on those fronts.

The scientists explored what would happen if they genetically deleted the warmth-detector protein. In male mice, this reduced their avoidance of the warmer plate, suggesting this protein normally sends a signal that discourages them from staying on warmer surfaces. The mice's preferred temperature also rose to about 95 F (35 C), closer to that of females.

The study suggests that testosterone somehow tweaks the function of heat-sensing nerves in the skin.

In female mice, deleting or blocking the protein did not have any significant effect.

The team then tried eliminating or blocking the coolness-detecting protein, finding that males and females didn't avoid the cool plates as strongly as they did before. Female mice also spent less time on the warmer plates, but males' preference for the warmer plates didn't change.

"Females are a little bit more responsive to activation of the cold receptor," Caterina said, "and a little bit less responsive to activation of the warmer receptor." That's despite the temperature-sensing neurons in both sets of mice working identically, the team found.

The researchers suspected that sex hormones might help to explain this difference.

They gave a group of male mice a drug that blocks the production of testosterone. Weeks after the treatment, these mice spent more time on the 38 C plate than males with normal testosterone. Meanwhile, female mice given testosterone lost their preference for warmer temperatures.

Interestingly, giving male mice female hormones, including forms of estrogen and progesterone, did not affect their temperature preferences. And blocking the hormones in female mice also had no effect. These hormones are known to influence other aspects of temperature regulation in the body, though, such as heat dissipation through the skin; but in this case, they didn't seem to affect animals' perception of temperature.

"So it really seems as though testosterone is the most important determinant," McNaughton said. But these changes were only partial; testosterone did not completely reverse the differences between the sexes. "So there is something else going on that we weren't able to identify," he added.

The exact mechanism for how testosterone impacts the sensor proteins is not clear. Because the effect happened over weeks, researchers suggested that it did not directly affect the temperature-sensing proteins. It might instead act indirectly by influencing the activity of genes, but further studies would be needed to confirm this idea.

Although the researchers did not conduct any tests in humans, McNaughton noted that the same sensor proteins are present in people and that studies with humans suggest that they behave in a similar way.

This research provides "valuable information" for understanding how the proteins responsible for sensing temperature work, Caterina said. Understanding these mechanisms could be useful for studying conditions like neuropathic pain, in which people's sensitivity to heat and cold is enhanced.

"What kinds of signals create our daily experiences around temperature is by itself very important," he told Live Science. "It's a big part of understanding ourselves as living beings."

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

Vilar, B., & McNaughton, P. A. (2026). TRPM8 and TRPM2 ion channels determine sex differences in thermal preference in mice. The Journal of Physiology. https://doi.org/10.1113/jp288076

#6343. Modern life is changing the DNA of bacteria in our guts

Gut bacteria can acquire genes from neighboring microbes, adding to the genetic differences linked to how people live.

Diet, antibiotics, and indoor plumbing help shape which bacteria settle into a person’s gut. That much has been clear for years.

What researchers couldn’t say is whether the bacteria themselves have been evolving in response.

A study of nearly 6,000 gut bacterial genomes finds that they have.

Across the species examined, strains from industrialized communities carried more genes than those from non-industrialized communities.

Most of the extra genes arrived recently. The bacteria didn’t inherit them from a parent cell. They took them from other microbes living alongside them.

So modern life hasn’t only changed which bacteria live in the gut. The same species now carries a different set of genes depending on how its host lives.

Researchers at Kiel University’s Institute of Clinical Molecular Biology and MIT’s Department of Biological Engineering ran the work, with the evolutionary modeling done in Japan.

Everything here was measured in bacterial genomes, so none of it shows that a bigger bacterial genome makes a person healthier or sicker.

All of the genomes come from the Global Microbiome Conservancy, a non-profit effort to bank living strains from communities that microbiome research has mostly passed over.

For this study, 20 volunteers in Cameroon, Ghana, Malaysia, Nigeria and Rwanda gave fresh stool samples. None had taken antibiotics recently.

Scientists processed each sample on site within three hours. The samples were then frozen in liquid nitrogen at minus 321°F (minus 196°C).

In the lab, the material went onto plates inside an oxygen-free chamber. Colonies grew at 99°F (37°C) for one to two weeks. Single colonies were then picked and sequenced.

The cultures yielded 1,841 new bacterial genomes. Added to 4,140 strains already banked, the collection reached 5,981 genomes. They came from 56 donors in nine countries.

Researchers classified donors as industrialized or non-industrialized using a development score for where they lived, compared with their country’s median.

From that collection, the team picked ten species sampled well on both sides of the divide, with at least eight strains from each side. Most are Bacteroides and close relatives, the workhorses of the lower gut.

E. coli was left out on purpose. Its genetic diversity has already been mapped in detail.

In all ten species, strains from industrialized guts carried more protein-coding genes. The difference was statistically significant in eight of the ten species.

Core genes, the ones every strain of a species has, showed no difference. The extra material was all optional genes, the kind one strain carries and the next one doesn’t.

The optional sets also varied more from strain to strain in industrialized hosts, again in all ten species. The team then widened the comparison to 34 species and saw the same pattern.

A bigger genome could mean two different things. Either these strains picked up genes lately, or strains that already had big genomes happened to do well in modern guts.

Separating the two fell to a group in Okinawa, Japan. They compared the family tree of a single gene with the family tree of the species carrying it.

A mismatch between the two marks the spot where a gene was gained, lost or handed over.

Gene gains clustered near the tips of the evolutionary trees, indicating that they occurred relatively recently.

They also piled up on the branches belonging to industrialized hosts.

Between 80% and 90% of those gains were transfers from other microbes. Only a small share came down from a parent cell.

Many arrived packaged inside plasmids and viruses that infect bacteria.

Both deliver several genes at once. Swapping of this kind goes on well beyond the gut, in soil, seawater and thawing permafrost.

Gergely Szöllősi heads the Model-Based Evolutionary Genomics Unit at the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology.

His group built these tools for a much older problem, and Lénárd Szánthó, a senior bioinformatician in the unit, adapted them to a far shorter stretch of time.

“These methods were built to look back hundreds of millions and billions of years, so it was not obvious that they would tell us anything about something this recent,” said Szöllősi.

“Lénárd made them work for this problem, and the picture that comes out is that bacteria in industrialized hosts have been acquiring genes from their neighbors recently, and this is what makes their genomes larger.”

About 5% of the gene families in a typical species collection tracked with the host’s way of life.

The team checked that against bacterial DNA read straight from the stool of 1,015 people, and 83% of the signals pointed the same way.

A few gene families turned up in more than one species, which is harder to put down to chance.

Two of them help build the outer coat of the cell, the part that other microbes and the immune system meet.

Another repeat hit was an enzyme that breaks down penicillin-type drugs. Genes like that ride the same mobile DNA now spreading antibiotic resistance through cities and farms.

The team also counted genes where protein-changing mutations had built up faster than mutations that did not change the protein. That pattern is the usual sign of a change being favored.

About 1.4% of the genes examined qualified. One of them helps a cell hold its outer envelope together under stress, and it carried the signature in three separate species.

In the five species with the most genomes, the researchers tracked single-letter DNA differences in core genes.

The variants tied to industrialized hosts kept landing on the same few jobs: building the cell wall, handling stress and making vitamin B12.

A companion study from the same group found more vitamin B12 production in the gut communities of people more exposed to industrialized environments.

Another cluster of changes hit the genes that build a molecule on the bacterial surface. The human immune system reads that molecule and reacts to it.

Researchers have not tested whether any of this changes how a person’s immune system behaves. The authors wrote that it is a possibility worth following up.

“I hope our results will inspire further studies to use this knowledge in supporting us to live a healthier life in our changing environment,” Szánthó said.

The analysis can’t say which part of industrialized living is responsible. Diet, medicine, sanitation and exposure to outdoor microbes all travel together, and this data can’t pull them apart.

Bigger genomes may not be an adaptation at all.

Extra genes build up on their own when the pressure to discard useless DNA eases, and the authors couldn’t rule that out.

Ten species is a thin slice of a gut that holds hundreds, and most of the ten belong to one bacterial group.

Species that have never been grown in a lab are missing here, which matters because industrialized guts hold fewer bacterial species to begin with.

The study itself doesn’t test what those extra genes actually do inside a person. Getting that answer will take experiments rather than more genomes.

The authors call for controlled experiments with bacteria, laboratory studies of evolution, and more detailed measurements of people’s living conditions.

The full study was published in the journal Cell.

#6342. How I Got My Visa to France

I’ve been in love with France ever since my first trip to Bordeaux in 2010. Friends I had met back in Thailand showed me around the area and introduced me to French culture. It was my first time in France and I loved the food, the wine, and the people.

But that love became an obsession when, after Bordeaux, I stepped out of the Paris metro and onto the Champs-Élysées. The lights, the energy, the mystique! There was magic in the air. I felt like I had known the city my entire life and I was simply returning home.

Since then, Paris has had a firm grip on my heart. Over the years, I spent countless visits exploring France and Paris in particular. I’ve run tours in the city and I spent a few months living there in 2019.

Last August, after yet another sojourn, I thought to myself, “What if I moved back?”

I was growing a bit tired of the NYC dating scene, the rising cost of living, and felt like, creatively, I was in a rut. With AI coming for creators like me and the industry changing, I was a little lost on what, career-wise, would come next.

And Paris seemed like the best place to go.

It’s cheaper than NYC, I had friends there already, I’ve always wanted to learn French, it would make a great base for exploring Europe, and I could start writing my next book there. There’s nothing like a change in scenery to get the creativity flowing!

But the question remained: how do you move to France?

After all, they don’t have a digital nomad visa, and you’re limited to three months if you visit on your regular Schengen tourist visa.

Well, it turns out that it’s not actually that hard. (And while I can only speak for Americans, I suspect the criteria are similar for Canadians, Aussies, Kiwis, and other “developed” nations.)

If you want to move to France, you have four main options:

The student visa is pretty straightforward. You need to enroll in a full-time university program and show you have enough funds to support yourself (around 600 Euros per month). A friend is currently there on this visa, as she is doing a nine-month intensive French program to become fluent. You still have to apply for the visa, but if you’re enrolled in an accredited school, you’ll likely get approved. Another benefit to this visa is that you can work part-time on it!

But this visa is contingent on being in school, so if you leave or quit, it’s voided. However, when you are done, you can change this to a “job seeker” visa, which can give you up to another six months in France (or more depending on how long your program was).

I thought about applying for the entrepreneur visa, but the application process is pretty complex and can take months to be approved. You have to set up your business in France — and that is a lot of paperwork. You have to show that your business makes money, has clients (at least one of them being French), and can support you full-time (you have to make at least the French minimum wage). They will scrutinize your assets and financials a lot and you’ll need to register your business in France and pay French taxes.

Additionally, France offers a talent visa. If you’re an expert in your field (with verifiable accreditations and accolades), this could be a good visa to apply for, especially if you plan to stay in France for a long time and want to physically work there. But, again, you’ll need to have some source of income and plan to do physical business in France. If you’re not an academic but someone in the arts, you have to show how you are going to add to the “culture of France” in some way.

While I would meet the requirements for both those visas, the process for either would have been time-consuming, and, since I’m not sure France is going to be my forever home, I decided not to go through that process.

So I went with the long-term visitor visa, officially called VLS-TS visiteur. This allows me to stay up to 12 months in France and is renewable in the country. It does come with a lot of restrictions, however: I can’t physically work here and I am not allowed into the French social welfare system.

It’s also the visa a lot of Americans (and most retirees) are coming in on. If you have passive income or retirement savings and just want to live in France, this is a good option for you. It allows you to set up a bank account and it can be renewed pretty much indefinitely.

The paperwork for this visa (which I’ll get into in a bit) essentially comes down to whether or not you can support yourself. French authorities want to make sure you won’t be a burden on the system.

My biggest question centered around whether or not I could “work” on this visa. A lot of creators and digital nomads are applying for — and getting — this visa.

But remember: you aren’t allowed to work on this visa so how are you going to work if you can’t work?

So let me take a moment to talk about “work” from a legal standpoint.

As I mentioned, there’s no digital nomad visa that allows you to work in France. And the French tax office said last July that remote work is considered taxable — but there are no official laws that say so. That’s just their opinion and there’s been no progress in codifying that opinion. In fact, my visa doesn’t even come with a tax number, so I can’t be taxed. I couldn’t pay taxes even if I wanted to.

The visa office asks how you’ll support yourself when you are in France and one of the sources of income they accept is “income from work.” I was very open that my means of support would be the income from this blog and my books.

The system there really hasn’t caught up to remote work. It still defines “work” as something you do physically that could take away a job from a French person.

So could I run walking tours in Paris? Nope. Could you work at a café? Nope.

But does writing this blog post count as work? After all, no one is paying for it. It’s a free resource. Does going to a café to work on the next great American novel count? What about my weekly newsletter that has affiliate links (that generate income) in it? Is writing that considered work?

The gray area is considerable, so the best thing to do is to talk to a lawyer. I recommend Daniel Tostado (yes, that’s his real name), one of the biggest American-French immigration lawyers in Paris. He has a huge law firm and regularly meets with government officials to clarify the rules on this. He gave me some solid advice.

For this long-term visitor visa, the application process is pretty easy. You go to the French government website, fill out your application, take the application number to the TLScontact website, and make an appointment. (France outsources the appointment process to this company, which then sends everything to the French consulate for approval.)

The main things you’ll want to demonstrate are that you have accommodation for 90 days on your application and enough income to support yourself. They just want to make sure you aren’t going to be a burden on the system. I went overboard. Here’s what I brought to my appointment:

I didn’t need the second bank account, tax returns, or W-2 (they weren’t required) but the woman at the appointment said the more proof you had the better and it wouldn’t hurt. And another friend who got this visa didn’t bring anything beyond what was asked in the application form. But I wanted to take no chances!

At the appointment, the staff double-checks your paperwork, takes your biometric data, collects the fees, and then sends your passport to the embassy for processing. Officially, it takes up to 15 days to process your visa, but everyone I know seems to get it back within a week.

The worst part was not knowing if you are approved until your passport is returned. While you can track the progress of your application, you don’t know the verdict until your passport is back in your hands. While I was waiting (and anxiously spiraling), I looked on Reddit and found that most denials were for lack of income or issues with their accommodation, which seem to be the two most important things to have perfect on your application.

Once you get your visa back, you can enter France any time after the start date. After you enter, you have 90 days to register your visa with the state (they give you a little QR code with instructions). This allows you to “officially” be on this long-term visa. (It’s a more paperwork kind of thing.)

Once that is done, there’s nothing else to do and you can stay in France (and Europe) until your visa expires!

So, if you’re considering moving to France, these are your options. But, as always, I’m not a lawyer and this is not legal advice. In regard to work and other issues or questions, it’s important that you seek legal counsel and get their expert opinion!

#6341. 2026 Full Moon calendar: When to see the Full Moon and phases

The phenomenon of a Full Moon arises when our planet, Earth, is precisely sandwiched between the Sun and the Moon. This alignment ensures the entire side of the Moon that faces us gleams under sunlight. Thanks to the Moon’s orbit around Earth, the angle of sunlight hitting the lunar surface and being reflected back to our planet changes. That creates different lunar phases.

The next Full Moon will be the November Beaver Moon, which occurs at 9:54 a.m. EST on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026. It will also be a Super Moon.

We’ll update this article multiple times each week with the latest moonrise, moonset, Full Moon schedule, and some of what you can see in the sky each week.

Here’s the complete list of Full Moons this year and their traditional names.

(All times Eastern; * denotes a Super Moon.)

The images below show the day-by-day phases of the Moon in November. The Full Moon this month will be on Tuesday, Nov. 24, 2026.

The times below for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location. All other times are Eastern unless otherwise specified. For more details on upcoming sky events, check out our full Sky This Week column.

Sunrise: 6:35 A.M.Sunset: 4:52 P.M.Moonrise: 3:56 A.M.Moonset: 3:16 P.M.Moon Phase: Waning crescent (5%)

Saturday, November 7This morning, the Moon passes 1.1° due south of Venus at 7 A.M. EST. You can spot the pair an hour before sunrise, some 6° high in the east and climbing as the sky begins to brighten. Magnitude –4.5 Venus blazes to the upper left of the delicate crescent Moon, whose western limb is just barely lit as the Sun sets across the lunar nearside. Look for earthshine on the already-shadowed portion of Luna’s face, as sunlight bouncing off Earth lights it up. Near Venus is another bright light: This is Spica, Virgo’s alpha star, shining at magnitude 1.0 and also lingering in the morning twilight.

Sunrise: 6:36 A.M.Sunset: 4:51 P.M.Moonrise: 5:01 A.M.Moonset: 3:40 P.M.Moon Phase: Waning crescent (1%)

Tuesday, November 10The waxing crescent Moon passes 0.3° south of Antares at midnight EST, although the pair is not visible at that time. You can catch our satellite setting in the west around sunset, although it will likely disappear before Antares pops out of the twilight only shortly before the star itself sets as well.

Sunrise: 6:43 A.M.Sunset: 4:45 P.M.Moonrise: 10:54 A.M.Moonset: 7:55 P.M.Moon Phase: Waxing crescent (21%)

The phases of the Moon are: New Moon, waxing crescent, First Quarter, waxing gibbous, Full Moon, waning gibbous, Last Quarter, and waning crescent. A cycle starting from one Full Moon to its next counterpart, termed the synodic month or lunar month, lasts about 29.5 days.

Though a Full Moon only occurs during the exact moment when Earth, Moon, and Sun form a perfect alignment, to our eyes, the Moon seems Full for around three days.

There are a wide variety of specialized names used to identify distinct types or timings of Full Moons. These names primarily trace back to a blend of cultural, agricultural, and natural observations about the Moon, aimed at allowing humans to not only predict seasonal changes, but also track the passage of time.

For instance, almost every month’s Full Moon boasts a name sourced from Native American, Colonial American, or other North American traditions, with their titles mirroring seasonal shifts and nature’s events.

Wolf Moon (January): Inspired by the cries of hungry wolves.

Snow Moon (February): A nod to the month’s often heavy snowfall.

Worm Moon (March): Named after the earthworms that signal thawing grounds.

Pink Moon (April): In honor of the blossoming pink wildflowers.

Flower Moon (May): Celebrating the bloom of flowers.

Strawberry Moon (June): Marks the prime strawberry harvest season.

Buck Moon (July): Recognizing the new antlers on bucks.

Sturgeon Moon (August): Named after the abundant sturgeon fish.

Corn Moon (September): Signifying the corn harvesting period.

Hunter’s Moon (October): Commemorating the hunting season preceding winter.

Beaver Moon (November): Reflects the time when beavers are busy building their winter dams.

Cold Moon (December): Evocative of winter’s chill.

In addition, there are a few additional names for Full Moons that commonly make their way into public conversations and news.

Super Moon: This term is reserved for a Full Moon that aligns with the lunar perigee, which is the Moon’s nearest point to Earth in its orbit. This proximity renders the Full Moon unusually large and luminous. For a Full Moon to earn the Super Moon tag, it should be within approximately 90 percent of its closest distance to Earth.

Blue Moon: A Blue Moon is the second Full Moon in a month that experiences two Full Moons. This phenomenon graces our skies roughly every 2.7 years. Though the term suggests a color, Blue Moons aren’t truly blue. Very occasionally, atmospheric conditions such as recent volcanic eruptions might lend the Moon a slightly blueish tint, but this hue isn’t tied to the term.

Black Moon: A Black Moon is a recent, unofficial term that can describe one of two situations. Either the third of four New Moons in a single astronomical season or the second of two New Moons in a month is a Black Moon. As its name suggests, the Black Moon is completely dark, as it is a New Moon that occurs when the Moon is between the Sun and Earth. The New Moon cannot be observed except during a total solar eclipse.

Harvest Moon: Occurring closest to the autumnal equinox, typically in September, the Harvest Moon is often renowned for a distinct orange tint it might display. This Full Moon rises close to sunset and sets near sunrise, providing extended hours of bright moonlight. Historically, this was invaluable to farmers gathering their produce.

What is the difference between a Full Moon and a New Moon? A Full Moon is witnessed when Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, making the entire Moon’s face visible. Conversely, during a New Moon, the Moon lies between Earth and the Sun, shrouding its Earth-facing side in darkness.

How does the Full Moon influence tides? The Moon’s gravitational tug causes Earth’s waters to bulge, birthing tides. During both Full and New Moons, the Sun, Earth, and Moon are in alignment, generating “spring tides.” These tides can swing exceptionally high or low due to the combined gravitational influences of the Sun and Moon.

#6340. Record-low temperature created on China’s space station

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A Bose-Einstein condensate reached about 10 trillionths of a kelvin

An experiment on China's Tiangong space station (rendering shown) reached a record-low temperature in a state of matter called a Bose-Einstein condensate.

Shujianyang/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Science has reached a new low. Temperature, that is.

Scientists cooled a collection of atoms to about 10 picokelvins, or 10 trillionths of a kelvin. That’s barely a smidge above absolute zero (−273.15° Celsius). The atoms formed a Bose-Einstein condensate, a quantum state of matter, colder than any before, researchers report November 5 in Science.

To achieve that record-low chill, scientists took their work to space. The atoms orbited Earth aboard China’s Tiangong space station. There, researchers used laser-based traps to contain 20,000 rubidium atoms and reduce their motion, thereby cooling them. At an atomic level, temperature is tied to motion: Atoms and molecules in the air around us move more slowly when it’s colder. Similarly, in systems of cold atoms, scientists can define an effective temperature based on how slowly the atoms spread apart when they are allowed to expand.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

On Earth, gravitational forces cause clouds of atoms to sag, reducing the effectiveness of cooling. But on the space station, the atoms experienced microgravity, the apparent weightlessness of an object in free fall.

To make a Bose-Einstein condensate, a disorderly gaggle of atoms is cooled until the atoms all take on the same quantum state, acting as one entity. By experimenting with ultracold atoms, researchers can study exotic states of matter and other mysterious physics. And they can test fundamental concepts, such as the equivalence principle — the idea that explains why objects of different masses fall at the same rate in a vacuum.

Spacefaring Bose-Einstein condensates were previously made on the International Space Station, at effective temperatures as low as 52 picokelvins. And an experiment on Earth, in which atoms were dropped down a tower to induce weightlessness, reached 38 picokelvins. But drop tower experiments are limited by the time their free fall lasts. That’s not an issue for experiments in Earth’s orbit. So cold atoms in space are really taking off.

Nature Communications. 2022. doi: 10.1038/s41467-022-35274-6C. Deppner et al. Collective-mode enhanced matter-wave optics. Physical Review Letters. 2021. doi: 10.1103/PhysRevLett.127.100401

#6339. Rescuers nursed a green sea turtle back to health and watched it swim almost 2,000 miles with a satellite tag

A rehabilitated green sea turtle nicknamed 3K swam nearly 1,860 miles (3,000 km) in four months, from Northland to Wellington and back.

On the afternoon of March 12, 2025, five rehabilitated green sea turtles were let go in Rangaunu Harbour, in the far north of New Zealand. Two of the five had satellite tags on their shells.

By now 11 turtles have been tagged. One of them, nicknamed 3K, clocked up nearly 1,860 miles (3,000 kilometers) in four months.

It went from Rangaunu down the west coast to Wellington and back, the Department of Conservation (DOC) reported on October 29.

DOC put out the update together with Auckland Zoo and SEA LIFE Kelly Tarlton’s Aquarium in Auckland. No journal paper sits behind it. These are tracking results from 11 animals so far, and every one of them was a patient first.

Team Turtle is the name of the project. DOC leads it with Auckland Zoo and SEA LIFE Kelly Tarlton’s. Iwi, the Māori tribes of the area, work alongside them.

Since 2025, each of the 11 has been tracked daily for six to 12 months. The location data go through Kinéis, a new network of 25 satellites, which DOC says gives highly accurate positions. The transmitters were meant to last up to a year.

Back in 2025, DOC said this was the largest satellite tagging study ever undertaken for green turtles in New Zealand. The plan was to tag up to 20 turtles over three years.

That same year Andrew Christie, curatorial manager at Kelly Tarlton’s, said the aquarium had rehabilitated more turtles than ever before.

Five species of turtle are seen in New Zealand waters, and green and leatherback turtles are the most common. Dr. Karen Middlemiss leads the project as a marine senior science advisor at DOC.

Green turtles don’t breed in New Zealand, she said, yet juveniles and sub-adults show up regularly in the warmer North Island waters. She compared the country to “a baby-sitting service for teenagers” before they head back to Pacific nesting beaches.

3K left Rangaunu Harbour and followed the west coast south until it reached Wellington, at the foot of the North Island.

On the way home it spent a month in Manukau Harbour, on the Auckland side. The round trip added up to nearly 1,860 miles (3,000 kilometers) in four months.

A second turtle, released at Taupō Bay in Northland, took the other side. It went down the east coast as far as the Coromandel, turned around, and settled in Rangaunu Harbour.

Before the tags, the team knew very little about individual turtles, Middlemiss said. Nobody knew if individuals stayed in one place for long periods or kept moving to other parts of the country. In the Galápagos, tags showed some green turtles remain homebodies for months.

Nesting females tagged on Diego Garcia, in the Indian Ocean, do not always swim straight to their feeding grounds.

DOC picked out several places from the tracks for future work. In Northland these are Rangaunu Bay and Harbour, Pārengarenga Harbour, Murimotu, Whangārei Harbour and the Bay of Islands. Manukau Harbour in Auckland is on the list too.

Turtles that spent most of their time in Rangaunu Harbour were most often located over seagrass and harbour channels. Green turtles eat mostly seaweed, seagrasses and algae, according to NOAA Fisheries. Some have gone back to the same seagrass meadows for about 3,000 years.

Two iwi, Ngāti Kahu and Ngāi Takoto, whakapapa (trace their ancestry) to Rangaunu. Wiremu Marsden, Ngāi Takoto Taiao Team Lead, said in 2025 that honu, the Māori word for sea turtles, have always been in the harbour.

Nina Raharuhi is hapū (subtribe) cultural monitor for Ngāti Kahu, with Ngāti Whātua affiliation. In 2025 she said the honu come in from the subtropical islands for a rest, shelter and food before they go off to breed.

The strandings of the previous two years worried her. She wondered if water temperature, lack of food, what was in their food or microplastics were to blame.

This October she said the release of the 11 honu “represents hope, healing, and our shared responsibility as kaitiaki,” or guardians. Her message to boaters and fishers on the harbour: “Ata haere, kia tūpato,” which she translated as take it easy and be careful.

Dr. James Chatterton is the veterinary services manager at Auckland Zoo. August to December is the busy stretch for sick turtles at the zoo, he said, and eight had come in since June.

The cases he listed were fishhooks, line entanglement and boat strikes. Pneumonia and intestinal infections turn up too, usually after the turtle’s immune system has been knocked down. His guess is that less food, a damaged marine environment, or both, are behind that.

“The good news is more than two-thirds of the green sea turtles we admit go on to make a full recovery,” Chatterton said. He wants the sea itself to improve so that more of them do well once they are back in it.

SEA LIFE Kelly Tarlton’s general manager, Dan Henderson, said the results show how linked New Zealand’s marine habitats are. His aquarium plans to use them to show visitors what ocean animals face.

DOC gave boaters four tips: slow down and keep the boat off the plane where turtles live, wear polarized sunglasses, name a spotter, and fit a propeller guard.

An injured or stranded turtle should be reported to 0800 DOCHOT, DOC’s hotline. People should not handle it unless DOC staff say so, and all sea turtles in New Zealand waters are threatened.

Eleven turtles have been followed, six to 12 months each, and every one was a rescue animal. In March 2025 DOC noted that young turtles are hard on tags in coastal waters and can knock them off early.

The maps give positions and dates. They give no reason for 3K’s trip to Wellington, and none for the Taupō Bay turtle settling in Rangaunu. Chatterton’s idea about food and immunity is a suspicion at the zoo, not a result of the tracking.

To reach 20 turtles, Team Turtle will tag nine more, working with iwi and hapū. Middlemiss said regional councils are next on the list, to talk about getting turtles into coastal management plans.

In Western Australia, satellite tags helped scientists map where green turtles feed and migrate. The next turtles to leave rehab with a tag will be followed the way 3K was, to Wellington and back.

The information was obtained from the Department of Conservation.

A double subduction zone off the coast of Japan caused rifting halfway around the world to accelerate, fueling the formation of some of North America's most iconic features.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A geological reorganization near Japan may have led to the formation of one of North America's most recognizable features.

The birth of the Gulf of California, which rifted from Mexico and created the Baja Peninsula 6 million to 8 million years ago, was accelerated by the formation of a double subduction zone more than 6,000 miles (9,600 kilometers) away, near Japan. This reorganization led to a transfer of tectonic force across the Pacific tectonic plate, which, in turn, opened the Gulf of California and ultimately led to the Grand Canyon's formation, according to new research published Oct. 29 in the journal Science.

The findings will help researchers understand more about plate boundaries, which is where most of the strongest earthquakes on the planet originate.

"It's more than a regional curiosity," study co-author Thorsten Becker, a geophysicist at the University of Texas at Austin (UT Austin), told Live Science. "It's a reminder of the global connectedness of mantle convection and plate tectonics."

The Gulf of California is an example of a rift zone, a place where continental crust pulls apart and creates a spot so low that it can be filled by ocean water. There are many rift zones around the world; a currently active one is the Red Sea. But rifting can slow down, speed up or peter out entirely. In the Gulf of California, rifting not only persisted, but sped up. Rifting took about 6 million to 13 million years ‪—‬ much quicker than the typical speed of 30 million to 80 million years.

Study co-author Guido Gianni, a geophysicist at the Czech Academy of Sciences, wondered why that was. No previous research fully explained the rapid rifting, which changed the face of North America in many ways. Not only did the rifting transfer Baja California to the Pacific Plate, but it provided an outlet for the developing Colorado River, which subsequently carved the Grand Canyon on its way to sea level.

Gianni and Becker's doctoral student at UT Austin, Xiang He, used a global model of plate tectonics, run on supercomputers at the Texas Advanced Computing Center on campus, to find out if far-flung forces might provide an explanation. Around the same time the Gulf of California was pulling apart, Japan was undergoing its own geological changes. Off the coast of Japan, the Pacific Plate subducts, or pushes under, the Eurasian Plate. About 10 million to 12 million years ago, a single subduction zone near Japan transitioned into two separate subduction zones.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

A double subduction zone off Japan (left inset) accelerated the growth of the Gulf of California (right inset).

This transition at the western end of the Pacific Plate influenced the tectonic forces on the other side of the plate, He, Gianni, Becker and their colleagues found.

"It turned out — ta-da! — [with] the change in this pulling stress, Baja California was one of the few places outside the Japan region that were affected," Becker said. It was "unexpected and sort of a little bit too good to be true."

The researchers tweaked their model to see if the result held with different assumptions about stresses and mantle properties, and it did.

"It turned out — ta-da! — [with] the change in this pulling stress, Baja California was one of the few places outside the Japan region that were affected," Becker said. It was "unexpected and sort of a little bit too good to be true."

The researchers tweaked their model to see if the result held with different assumptions about stresses and mantle properties, and it did.

The Gulf of California was already rifting regardless of the situation across the Pacific. The initial rift was caused by the subduction of a tectonic plate called the Farallon Plate, located under the West Coast of North America. The Farallon slab stretched and thinned the continental crust of the North American plate as it moved. But such rifting might have ended with nothing more than the formation of a little valley or low spot if Japan's influence had not kicked in to give the rifting some extra oomph.

The findings have a direct effect on scientists' understanding of how plate boundaries form, Becker said. And this isn't just academic. The findings could have implications for understanding earthquake-generating faults such as the San Andreas in California and the Cascadia subduction zone in the Pacific Northwest, Becker said. Cascadia is what's known as a "megathrust" boundary, capable of triggering quakes of more than magnitude 9.

"If I'm asking what is the mantle doing underneath Cascadia so I get our megathrust correct," Becker said, "I need to include these effects."

Gianni, G. M., He, X., Becker, T. W., & Faccenna, C. (2026). Western Pacific double subduction drives Gulf of California rifting. Science, 394(6823), 515–519. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aef5187
