#6337. A biology student hunting for shark teeth found a stone spear point up to 4,500 years old

A Mary Baldwin student looking for shark teeth on Virginia's Eastern Shore found an ancient 6-inch spear point.

On Sept. 21, 2026, Brooklyn Rolph had a few spare minutes on a barrier island on Virginia’s Eastern Shore. The Mary Baldwin University biology major used them to scan the shell-covered ground for shark teeth, and instead she pulled a stone spear point out of the water.

It lay at the edge of an inlet with the tide coming in. The point measures about 6 inches (15 centimeters) long.

State archaeologists identified it as a Lehigh/Koens-Crispin point and put its age at 3,000 to 4,500 years, according to Mary Baldwin University. The Virginia Department of Historic Resources now holds the point and has not yet published its own description.

Rolph is a member of the class of 2028 from Hampton, Virginia. She was on a four-day field trip for her ecology course, BIOL 245, based at the University of Virginia’s Anheuser-Busch Coastal Research Center, a field station on the Eastern Shore that provides laboratory and dormitory facilities.

Paul Callo, Adam Seroka, Rebecca Haberman and Kadrin Anderson, all from the Mary Baldwin biology faculty, led the trip.

The island stop almost did not happen. Until the wind dropped, the class did not know whether the boats could go out at all, the university said.

The students spent the morning in wetsuits, wading through a seagrass bed and collecting specimens. Tides and currents then allowed only 35 to 40 minutes on a nearby barrier island, with a few free minutes after lunch.

Rolph had found small shark teeth on a beach trip years earlier, and the shells on this island looked promising. She told the university she was already “looking for something pointy.”

She spotted the point in the water at the edge of an inlet. Callo said the rising tide would soon have buried it.

“And then I pick it up, and I literally sprint to Dr. Seroka, because I’m like, wow, this is so crazy,” Rolph said.

Two friends nearby rushed over. Rolph said her professors were even more excited than she was.

Callo said he was “truly at a loss for words” when she showed it to him. He added that she was probably the first person to see and touch the point in thousands of years.

According to Rolph, the archaeologist who later examined it said he had never seen one in such good condition.

Callo warned Rolph that she might have to give the point up. The island is part of a natural area preserve owned by the Virginia Department of Conservation and Recreation, and the university says the class visited it with a state-issued permit.

Rolph showed the point to the research center’s site director, who made a phone call. The answer came back that the point belonged to the state.

Section 10.1-2303 of the Virginia Antiquities Act states that all objects of antiquity found on state-controlled land remain the property of the Commonwealth. The same section reserves field investigation on those sites to the director of historic resources.

Later that day, at the state archaeologist’s request, Conservation and Recreation staff picked up the point from the research center’s bunkhouse. They took it to the Virginia Department of Historic Resources for further study.

The Lehigh/Koens-Crispin type dates to the Late Archaic period. The Maryland Archaeological Conservation Laboratory cites a range of 2500 to 1700 BC from archaeologist Jay Custer, while other researchers give narrower spans.

The lab’s online guide describes a large, well-made point with a broad blade and a short stem that usually narrows toward the base. Makers shaped it by soft percussion, with little or no pressure retouching.

Archaeologists group these points with the broadspears (large, broad-bladed points), although the guide notes that many were used as knives. In samples from Maryland river valleys, most were made of quartzite or rhyolite, with fewer in quartz.

The type was first identified in 1916. Dorothy Cross named it in 1941 after the Koens-Crispin site, and W. Fred Kinsey combined it with the Lehigh point in 1972.

The guide lists lengths of 1.7 to 4.7 inches (44 to 120 millimeters). At about 6 inches, the Eastern Shore point is longer than that range.

The spear point was a surprise, but the rest of the trip ran as planned. The biology department makes the Eastern Shore trip every year, and each student designs and runs an experiment.

Rolph measured water turbidity, or cloudiness. She timed how fast filter feeders such as oysters and sea squirts cleared murky water, and she said running an experiment on her own was something she had not really done before.

Callo said the main goal is to let students explore coastal ecosystems that many have never seen before. He credited the research center’s staff with keeping the trip going each year.

The islands are studied by the Virginia Coast Reserve Long-Term Ecological Research program, which covers barrier islands, lagoons and marshes on the Eastern Shore.

A paper in Nature Geoscience predicts that barrier islands will disappear 50 percent faster than they have in the past, and other work shows that dunes stripped of vegetation may fail to recover.

The 3,000 to 4,500 year estimate comes from the point’s type, not from a laboratory date. Mary Baldwin’s account mentions no other objects, bones or charcoal found with it.

The university has not named the island. The Department of Historic Resources has not released a report on the point, its stone or any plan to display it.

Chance finds by students do sometimes reach specialists quickly. In July 2025, a Newcastle University archaeology student found a 1,100-year-old gold object within 90 minutes of her first dig in Northumberland, England.

Stone points also anchor much older questions, such as tools 13,500 to 20,000 years old that suggest the first Americans may have followed the Pacific coast.

For Rolph, the island stop began as a short search for shark teeth. Before the day was out, she had handed the point to the state.

The information was obtained from Mary Baldwin University.

#6336. Scientists figured out how to use engineered bacteria to dissolve rocks faster and capture carbon dioxide

Engineered ocean bacteria kept rust off olivine sand and sped up rock weathering, a slow process that pulls carbon dioxide into seawater.

As rock slowly wears away, it releases compounds that trap carbon dioxide and take it out of the atmosphere. The trouble is speed. Left alone, the process takes thousands of years, partly because iron in the rock turns to rust and coats the surface.

Now, a team led by Harvard researchers has engineered a common ocean bacterium to keep that rust from building up. In tanks of real harbor water, the microbes made crushed rock dissolve about three times faster than plain seawater did.

That’s a big jump for a process that has looked too slow to matter. So far the researchers have tested it only in lab reactors and a few glass tanks, not in the open ocean.

Neil Dalvie, a synthetic biology fellow in systems biology at Harvard Medical School, led the study with colleagues at the Wyss Institute and the Stanford Doerr School of Sustainability.

Dalvie told Earth.com he wanted to highlight the interdisciplinary nature of the work.

“We learned about alkalinity and mineral measurements from geochemists in the rock weathering industry,” he said. “Very few people have both the skillsets for molecular biology, microbial engineering, and mineral processing.”

“Some people describe rock weathering as a silver bullet for climate change,” said Dalvie. “The problem is that it’s too slow.”

The team worked with olivine, a common mineral, in the form of sand. When olivine dissolves in seawater, it gives off magnesium, silicon and iron.

The magnesium is the useful part. It makes seawater more alkaline, and alkaline seawater takes up carbon dioxide from the air. This is held as bicarbonate, a form of carbon dissolved in water.

Because magnesium stays in the ocean for a very long time, the authors count that carbon as stored for good.

Iron is the problem. It doesn’t stay dissolved. It forms a layer of rust on the rock, and that layer slows any further dissolving.

The rust is one reason that natural rock weathering takes so long. Spreading crushed rock on farm fields or coastlines helps, but the authors note that the carbon captured that way has been hard to measure.

Many microbes already have a way to deal with rust. When they run low on iron, they release molecules that grab iron and make it dissolve in water. Biologists call them siderophores.

Once a microbe has enough iron, though, it stops making these molecules. And a microbe doesn’t need much.

The team tested this with Alteromonas macleodii, a marine bacterium that makes its own siderophore. The researchers ran 16 small lab reactors with different amounts of olivine sand and different flow rates.

The bacteria made large amounts of the molecule only when there was little rock and the water moved fast.

With more rock, the bacteria had iron to spare and quit. The authors concluded that the bacterium’s natural settings rule out steady siderophore production in a tank big enough for industrial use.

So the team rewired the bacterium. They replaced the genetic switch that turns siderophore production on only when iron runs short with one that keeps it on all the time.

Dalvie said the change itself was fairly easy. Showing that it worked was the hard part.

“The bacteria keep growing, the cells keep making siderophores, the rock keeps dissolving – it’s very hard to measure all these things at the same time,” Dalvie said.

In the small reactors, the engineered strain produced more than 100 times as much of the siderophore as the natural strain. Olivine dissolved about 2.6 times faster with the engineered cells than in reactors with no cells at all, while the natural strain made no clear difference.

Then came a bigger test. The researchers placed more than 8.8 pounds (4 kilograms) of construction-grade olivine sand in the bottom of 3-gallon (11-liter) glass fish tanks.

Unfiltered seawater from Boston Harbor flowed through each tank at about 1.6 quarts (1.5 liters) a day. Some tanks got a slow drip of nutrients, and two of those also got a fresh dose of the engineered bacteria once a week.

In those two tanks, magnesium came off the rock 3.1 times faster. The water also became more alkaline, which the team calculated as about 0.018 ounce (0.50 grams) of carbon dioxide removed from the air each day.

That’s about half the weight of a paper clip. The amount is small, but it was measured directly in the water rather than estimated from a model.

In earlier small reactors fed raw seawater, the engineered strain held steady for about a week before its numbers fell. That’s why the pilot tanks got a fresh dose weekly.

The strain’s staying power surprised the team. “We were actually surprised that our originally engineered strains were able to survive and perform for over a week in unfiltered seawater,” Dalvie said.

“We think that biofilms may help protect the bacteria from growth competition and viruses in the seawater.”

Bacteria have to eat, and making their food releases carbon dioxide too. So the team ran a life-cycle analysis, an accounting of the emissions from building and running a full-size version.

Sugar failed on both counts. Making it emits too much, and in the lab, feeding it to the bacteria left the water less alkaline, likely because of acidic byproducts. The researchers switched to acetate, a simple food that some companies now make from carbon dioxide itself.

Ordinary bacteria failed the accounting too. Feeding wild microbes enough to keep them hungry for iron would release far more carbon dioxide than the faster weathering captured.

With engineered bacteria and a carbon-neutral acetate feed, the model predicted 74 percent more net carbon removal than a tank of rock and seawater alone. The researchers assumed the 2.6-fold speedup from the lab would hold at that scale.

“We’ve found a way that it could work and, maybe more importantly, now we have a model to calculate what it would look like to implement this at scale,” he said.

Four of the authors, Dalvie among them, have filed a patent application on strains of bacteria engineered for siderophore production that keep rust off rock.

The pilot tanks didn’t stay fast. After about three weeks of feeding, dissolving and carbon uptake dropped in every tank.

Slimy films of microbes had built up on the glass and on top of the sand, especially in the tanks that got the engineered bacteria.

The films appeared to keep the water from mixing, and the researchers suspect they blocked the rock. A thin crust had also formed, and most of the dissolving probably happened in the top 0.4 inch (1 centimeter) of sand.

The authors suggest that breaking up that top layer from time to time could keep the rock working, but they haven’t tested it. Dalvie and his colleagues say the next steps are larger experiments, better nutrient mixes and more efficient bacteria.

Dalvie said a real coastline or mine would need “some sort of enclosure or tank” to make enough of the iron-grabbing molecules. Such a tank “would resemble existing wastewater processes,” he said.

The bigger hurdle, he said, is the food for the bacteria. “Green feedstocks like this need to be available at large scales,” Dalvie said, referring to the acetate made from carbon dioxide and electricity.

The study did not analyze the economics of capturing carbon dioxide. “The price of carbon needs to be high enough to justify a new biochemical process,” he stressed.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Biotechnology.

#6335. Nov. 6, 1919: Einstein is right

The earliest test of Albert Einstein’s general theory of relativity took place just four years after he published it. During the May 29, 1919, total solar eclipse, British astronomer Sir Arthur Eddington and colleagues studied the theory by measuring how the Sun distorts light from background stars.

According to general relativity, any object with mass warps space-time. (The common analogy is that it’s similar to a bowling ball on a trampoline.) So, any passing body will follow a curved trajectory; this is true whether the passing body is an orbiting satellite or a light photon from a background object.

Researchers involved with the 1919 eclipse expedition traveled to two locations to observe totality: northern Brazil and a western island of Africa. According to general relativity, the apparent positions of stars near the Sun would appear to shift by 1.75 arcseconds. The scientists first measured the positions of stars in the Hydra star cluster in early 1919. Eddington and colleagues then recorded the stars’ locations during totality, and compared them to the previous values. They found that indeed, the background stars appeared to shift by roughly the amount general relativity had predicted. (They measured 1.98 arcseconds and 1.61 arcseconds.) The researchers announced their data on Nov. 6, 1919, and Einstein quickly became a household name.

Liz Kruesi is science writer with a background in physics who specializes in astronomy and space-related news.

#6334. Don’t Visit Ko Lipe

After 19 years, I finally went back to Ko Lipe, the Thai island I spent close to a month on in 2006. Back then, it was one of those super off-the-beaten-path destinations that few but the most intrepid travelers visited, where electricity only ran a few hours a day, basic bungalows right on the beach cost something like $2 USD, and there really was a last boat for the season.

There was much to do here but that was the point. You hung out on the beach, read a book, went snorkeling, went back to the beach, drank beers at the one beach bar on the island, rotated meals between the five restaurants there, and went to bed early.

It was paradise – and a place a lot of people got stuck. Days easily turned into weeks here.

If you asked me what the highlight of all my travels was, I would be the time I spent on Ko Lipe. I made incredible friends, lounged around, got to know the locals, learned a bit of Thai, and, overall, lived that idyllic backpacker life we all dream about.

Over the years, I’ve avoided going back to Ko Lipe because the memory of my time there is so strong that I didn’t want to ruin it. Any re-visit would simply be trying to recreated a magic that couldn’t be recreated because the people that it special wouldn’t be there. I’d be chasing travel ghosts. And, since I know my sleepy paradise has been developed greatly over the years, I was also too afraid seeing that would make me sad.

Tourism in Thailand tends toward the unsustainable. No island really develops in a good way. It’s all build, build, build.

And I didn’t want to see my Ko Lipe like that.

But as I was planning my recent trip through Southeast Asia, returning to Ko Lipe made sense. I was heading down the Indian Ocean side of Thailand on my way into Malaysia and I’d pass by it.

And, since I was looking for a lively place for New Year’s Eve, it seemed liked the best choice. I knew there would be travelers there and there were no other nearby islands that would work, especially since Ko Lipe has a boat to Langkawi, which was my next stop.

And I’m sad to report that Ko Lipe took the Ko Phi Phi model of tourism and is now extremely overdeveloped.

Most of the island is now paved over, the old dirt footpaths having become concrete for the cars and construction trucks. Swaths of palm trees are now the sites of high-end resorts with pools (on an island with no natural water supply). Construction of more resorts continues at a fast pace. The coral around the island is dying, a victim of all the boats, anchors, pollution, and overfishing. Beaches are now lined with boats, their exhaust spilling into the ocean, leaving a shiny film you can see as you swim. And the restaurants cater to tourists looking for bad Western food, not great Thai cuisine.

The island’s boom has displaced many locals, who were forced to sell to mainland developers, and much of the island’s workforce is now from the mainland. They see little of the benefits this tourism boom.

So lies Ko Lipe, another victim of Thailand’s all too common overdevelopment and exploitation of limited resources.

I met lots of people there who loved the island. If it’s your first time, I can see why you would love it. After all, the area is postcard perfect, the water is perfectly an azure blue, the sand is a beautiful white, and since you’re surrounded by a national park, a lot of tours take you to some secluded islands.

And, in comparison to Ko Phi Phi, Krabi, or Phuket, it is less developed so I can’t fault someone stepping here for the first time going “wow!”

But, as I reflect on the island and its overdevelopment, I have come to the same conclusion I have about Ko Phi Phi: people shouldn’t visit.

I’m not against growth, but I’m against this kind of growth. It’s not sustainably managed and going there will only tax the island’s limited resources even further. You can’t put the genie back in the bottle and no local is going to say “sure, I’ll stay broke so you can an idealized vision of the world.”

And, with so many other islands to visit that are well managed (Ko Lanta, Ko Jum, and Ko Mook, to name three nearby), I think you should skip Ko Lipe.

A visit there will only make things worse.

It pains me to say that, because it was such a beautiful place, and my original visit had a huge impact on my life. But if we’re going to be good stewards and travelers, sometimes you just have to say enough is enough.

And Ko Lipe is a place where enough is enough.

Go somewhere else that is better managed.

Riding elephants in Thailand went away when consumers became more conscious of it. Eco lodges got big because of consumers. Overtourism is talked about by consumers as much as it is by locals.

Maybe if enough people start to do something, Ko Lipe will change.

But, at the very least, by not going you are at least no contributing to the problem.

#6333. A man searching for a lost hammer in England accidentally discovered the richest Roman treasure ever found in Britain

In 1992, a search for a lost hammer in England uncovered the Hoxne Hoard, a Roman treasure containing 14,865 coins, gold jewelry and silverware.

On November 16, 1992, Eric Lawes was sweeping a field near Hoxne, in Suffolk, England, for a hammer that tenant farmer Peter Whatling had lost. His detector picked up ancient coins and silver spoons instead.

The find became known as the Hoxne Hoard. Together with coins recovered the following year, it holds 14,865 late Roman coins, along with gold jewelry and silver tableware.

The hoard is “the richest find of treasure from Roman Britain,” the British Museum says. Whatling’s hammer is now in its collection too.

Lawes, who lived in Hoxne, had received a metal detector as a retirement present, according to the Linda Hall Library.

Lawes and Whatling reported the find right away to Suffolk County Council, which owned the land.

Some objects had already been lifted, but Lawes stopped digging and left the rest for archaeologists.

The next day, a Suffolk Archaeological Unit team led by Judith Plouviez carried out a controlled emergency excavation of the remaining deposit.

The finds went to London for study the day after. The deposit had been lifted in small blocks of soil so that its layout could be recorded in the laboratory.

Catherine Johns and Roger Bland of the British Museum described these first steps in a 1994 report on the treasure.

The county’s Historic Environment Record lists 565 gold coins called solidi, 14,191 silver coins, most of them siliquae, and 24 bronze coins. Many of the silver coins had been clipped.

Another four gold solidi and 81 silver siliquae turned up in the plowed field in September 1993. That brought the totals to 569 gold coins and 14,272 silver coins, or 14,865 coins in all.

The gold jewelry included a body chain, six necklaces, three finger rings and 19 bracelets. One bracelet carries the words VTERE FELIX DOMINA IULIANE, a Latin good wish to a lady named Juliane.

The silver tableware included 78 spoons, 20 ladles, nine toilet implements, small bowls, a dish, two decorated vases, strainers, four pepper pots and a handle shaped like a tigress. A set of 10 spoons carries the name AVRVRSICINI, for Aurelius Ursicinus.

The four small bowls and the dish had been stacked together, possibly with hay and textile packing.

Fragments of ivory, bone inlay plates and two silver padlocks were also recovered.

The gold body chain measures about 33 inches (840 millimeters) when extended and weighs about 8.8 ounces (249.5 grams). Its complex loop-in-loop links form a flat strap rather than a round chain.

Its front setting holds an amethyst surrounded by four garnets, and four empty cells may once have held pearls. The clasp holds a gold coin of the emperor Gratian, struck between 367 and 375.

The body-chain type “had a long history” and appears in Hellenistic and Roman art, but “actual examples are extremely rare,” curators in London note. They estimate it fitted a slender woman or adolescent girl with a bust of about 30 to 32 inches (76 to 81 centimeters).

The so-called Empress pepper pot is a hollow silver half-figure of a woman, dated to between 300 and 400, about 4 inches (103 millimeters) tall, with gilded hair, jewelry and clothing.

A disc in its base could be turned to three positions: closed, open for filling and open for sprinkling pepper. The base rests on four small baluster feet.

The figure, which holds a gilded scroll in her left hand, probably represents a generic imperial image rather than a specific empress. Pepper reached the Roman world from India in the first century AD, and containers like this one are very rare finds.

The latest coins in the hoard are two of Constantine III, dated to 407 or 408.

The treasure was buried “for safety at a time when Britain was passing out of Roman control,” museum curators write. Its main container was presumably wooden, with iron nails and fittings along one edge.

The site also suffered extensive illicit digging, including trenching, in December 1992.

Geophysical surveys in 1993 revealed a single linear feature at the site.

In 1994, the Suffolk Archaeological Unit excavated a square about 98 feet (30 meters) across around the findspot. The dig found prehistoric and post-medieval features.

A coroner’s inquest in Lowestoft declared the hoard Treasure Trove on September 3, 1993. Under that ruling, the entire find went to the national collection.

Lawes received a finder’s reward of £1.75 million, which he shared with the tenant farmer.

The museum acquired the hoard in 1994 with major grants and many private donations.

By calling in the professionals, Lawes helped improve how archaeologists viewed metal detector users, the library notes.

The study was published in the journal Britannia.

Researchers found extreme levels of mercury in sediment cores in Mexico ‪—‬ and it’s all because the Maya loved red paint.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Maya used so much red paint that they accidentally poisoned their lakes and waterways with mercury, a new study finds.

The problem was cinnabar, a vivid-red mercury-sulfide mineral that can be used as the pigment vermilion in red paint. The run-off from the paint can enter waterways, where anaerobic bacteria then transform cinnabar into highly toxic methylmercury in the sediments of lakes. Over time, the methylmercury accumulates to higher levels in the food chain.

The ancient Maya, a people who lived in what is now southern Mexico and Central America and whose descendants are still around today, painted almost everything red. Archaeologists have found countless artifacts that the Maya reddened, including sculptures, monuments, walls, plazas, pottery and the dead for ceremonial funerals. Cinnabar was a common pigment in the paint they made, along with red ocher, which gets its color from a nontoxic iron mineral called hematite.

But the Maya passion for the color red — which to them represented the sun, blood and life — caused an environmental disaster when the nearby waters were poisoned by the cinnabar runoff, said study first author Matthew Waters, a paleolimnologist (a scientist who studies ancient waterways) at Auburn University in Alabama.

"They would have seen a strange color change in the water … and a drop in its productivity, such as fish for protein," he told Live Science. The Maya depended heavily on freshwater fisheries, including for freshwater shellfish.

Previous studies had already found evidence for high levels of mercury in the Maya's southern highlands and south-central lowlands, but no one had fully examined levels of the toxic mineral in Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula.

To investigate, Waters and his colleagues studied mercury levels in Maya-era mud in the Yucatán, and found overwhelming signs of mercury poisoning, probably from cinnabar paint, they reported in their study, published Nov. 4 in the journal Science Advances.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"We did not suspect [the Maya] used it in the quantities that we were seeing," he said.

The study found extreme levels of mercury in sediment cores from two Maya-era sites: Cobá Lake, a shallow lake beside the Maya city of that name, and Cenote Xcach (also spelled X-Canché), a flooded sinkhole beside a ruined city in the jungle that few have excavated.

The sediment cores chronicle the composition of earth and water over more than 2,000 years, and the times of mercury poisoning coincide with several periods during the Preclassic and Classic periods of the Maya civilization from about A.D. 40 to 820.

Waters explained that the Environmental Protection Agency in the U.S. has determined it is unsafe to drink water with mercury levels above 2 parts per billion, while the official limit for the level of mercury in fish, where it builds up over time, is 1 part per million — any number above that means the fish can be seized by authorities.

Severe poisoning occurs when the mercury levels in human blood exceed about 100 parts per billion, from drinking contaminated water or eating contaminated marine animals, such as fish. In humans, mercury poisoning can cause severe symptoms, including permanent lung damage, brain damage and death.

The reddish hue of the Maya sun god Kinich Ahau, made between the sixth and ninth centuries, now housed in Mexico’s National Museum of Anthropology, shows the Maya's love for mercury.

The most polluted parts of the Yucatan cores had a mercury level of 2.3 parts per million, the team discovered. "They experienced this for decades and, in one case, for centuries," Waters said.

The researchers then examined the sediment cores for signs of environmental damage caused by the mercury poisoning. They found that the cores lacked tiny fossils of freshwater shellfish, indicating that the high mercury levels were killing marine life. The team also noticed that the sediment cores had hardly any traces of algal blooms, which should have happened frequently, Waters said. That's likely because algae could not survive in the poisoned water nutrients.

Scholars debate why the Maya civilization collapsed in the eighth and ninth centuries, but a leading suspect is the disruption of food supplies caused by drought.

But although mercury levels were high during the Preclassic and Classic periods, the environmental damage caused by mercury levels had been falling in many places for hundreds of years by the time of the Maya collapse, Waters said, although it may have been a contributing factor.

Cinnabar does not occur naturally in the Yucatán, so it must have been imported there, probably from what's now Honduras, the researchers said. It seems these cinnabar imports eventually stopped at Cobá Lake, and the poisoning there fell to a background level of about 20 parts per billion by A.D. 520. However, the sediment cores showed that the mercury poisoning continued at Cenote Xcach until the collapse, they said.

Waters, M. N., Wooten, S. L., Abrook, A. M., Brenner, M., Curtis, J. H., Langdon, P. G., Medina-Gonzalez, R. M., Paradeisis-Stathis, S., & Vachula, R. S. (2026). Toxic mercury, aquatic ecosystem collapse, and the ancient Lowland Maya. Science Advances, 12(45), eaeh3280. https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.aeh3280

#6331. A warm winter melted the snow off a ‘grinning ice skull’ on Vega Island, and scientists say its jaw will soon shift

Landsat 9 images of Vega Island from March 2025 and October 2026 show a skull-shaped glacier stripped of snow after a winter that hit 59.7°F nearby.

On October 10, 2026, Landsat 9 passed over Vega Island, just east of the Antarctic Peninsula. From orbit, part of the island looks like a skull in profile, teeth showing, facing a little rock called Devil Island.

In that picture, large stretches of the face are gray instead of white. The snow that covered these glaciers in March 2025 was missing.

NASA Earth Observatory published the image on October 30 as “Vega Island Frozen in Fright.” Bare ice is easy to see from space. How much ice the glaciers lose in the coming summer has not been measured yet.

Lauren Dauphin of NASA Earth Observatory made the images from Landsat 9 data distributed by the U.S. Geological Survey. Lindsey Doermann wrote the story that ran with them.

NASA set the October view beside one from March 22, 2025. Clouds sat over the island in March 2026, so the comparison had to go back a year.

The eye socket is a nunatak, a rock peak poking up through the ice. The mouth is a lateral moraine, a line of rubble left along the side of a glacier. The jaw is Bahía del Diablo, or Devil’s Bay Glacier.

In the March 2025 image a layer of snow covers the ice. By October 2026 the snow is gone from wide areas. Darker glacier ice shows through across the face.

Mauri Pelto is a glaciologist at Nichols College in Dudley, Massachusetts. He told NASA that warm weather during the 2026 winter, mainly in June, was partly to blame for the bare ice.

He gave more detail on October 24 on his blog, From a Glacier’s Perspective. May, June, July and August were all warmer than average, he wrote. September was close to normal.

On the October 10 scene he marked several glaciers with snow on about half their surface or less. Some were on Vega Island and others on the western half of James Ross Island. He also found bare ice on the Eagle Island ice cap and on the Trinity Coast.

Esperanza Station is Argentina’s base on Hope Bay, at the northern tip of the peninsula. On June 5 and 6, 2026, it logged a high of 59.7°F (15.4°C). The figure comes from a paper in Advances in Atmospheric Sciences published September 18.

That was 34.4°F (19.1°C) above the station’s 1991 to 2020 average. The daily mean stayed above freezing for eight days starting June 3.

The authors blamed a blocking high-pressure system over the Drake Passage and Scotia Sea. It strengthened northwesterly winds over the peninsula and set off a foehn effect, a warm, dry wind blowing down the slope, on its eastern side.

On his blog, Pelto added that the gray patches do not mean the glaciers melted in winter. Little new snow fell, and wind scouring and sublimation, when snow turns straight into vapor, reduced it further.

“The winter season was no treat for these glaciers,” he said.

Bare ice is darker than snow and soaks up more sunlight, so Pelto expects faster melt if it persists. Wildfire soot darkened ice in the Rockies in a similar way. In the Arctic, red snow algae darken the ice.

According to Pelto, even a thin cover of new snow from a spring storm would help in the short run. Without it, the face on Vega Island will start to wear down.

“When entombed in snow and ice, the skull is preserved. But when exposed to melt, it weathers away, which will lead to a changing jawline and expanding eye socket,” Pelto said.

Jorge Rabassa and three colleagues made the first glacier inventory of James Ross and Vega islands. They used topographic maps, early Landsat images and aerial photos. Their 1982 paper in Annals of Glaciology counted 29 glaciers on Vega Island, NASA says.

Pedro Skvarca, one of those authors, later tracked Devil’s Bay Glacier with Hernán De Angelis and Evgeniy Ermolin.

Their 2004 paper reported an average yearly loss of about 1 foot (0.32 meters) of water equivalent from 1999 to 2003. The largest losses came in the two warmest summers.

The World Glacier Monitoring Service lists the glacier at 4.9 square miles (12.8 square kilometers) in 2025. It covered 5.5 square miles (14.3 square kilometers) in 2008. Between 2020 and 2022 its front moved back about 164 feet (50 meters) a year.

The Swedish Antarctic Expedition of 1901 to 1903 was led by Otto Nordenskjöld. NASA says the party split into three groups and lost its ship, the Antarctic, to pack ice.

Two of the groups reunited in 1903 at a point on Vega Island that became known as Cape Well-met. NASA places it off the forehead of the skull.

The cape was named for the meeting of a relief party led by Johan Gunnar Andersson with the winter party led by Nordenskjöld. The Argentine naval vessel Uruguay later rescued the survivors.

NASA’s comparison rests on two clear days, 19 months apart. Neither image measures snow depth or ice thickness. The 2026 to 2027 melt season is still ahead.

A few spring storms could still bury the gray patches. No field data from Devil’s Bay Glacier for this season had been published by early November.

Satellite images have shown that glaciers on the Antarctic Peninsula flow up to 22 percent faster in summer. For now, the skull still grins at Devil Island, with far less snow on its jaw than in March 2025.

The information was obtained from NASA Earth Observatory.

#6330. How octopuses squeeze through tiny openings, step by step

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The cephalopod how-to guide involves three or four moves, depending on a hole’s size

Octopuses are famous for fleeing tanks by squeezing through narrow slits and impossibly tiny holes. Now scientists have studied the sequences some cephalopods like this Mayan octopus use to make such great escapes.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Octopuses have made many a great escape. Remember Inky, who fled from New Zealand’s national aquarium?

The cephalopods can Houdini their way out of tanks and off boats by squeezing through narrow slits and incredibly tiny holes. Now researchers know exactly how some octopuses pull it off. These masterful getaways involve a consistent, step-by-step game plan, researchers report November 5 in the Journal of Experimental Biology.

Octopuses are mostly squishy muscle, allowing them to shape-shift, though they do have some rigid body parts. Not many scientists have studied how these animals squirm through small openings, says Robyn Crook, an evolutionary biologist at San Francisco State University who was not involved in the research. “It’s one of the most characteristic behaviors of octopuses in popular awareness, but the strategies octopuses use have not really been examined systematically.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Sneaking through small spaces isn’t just a party trick for octopuses, says Michael Kuba, a biologist at the University of Naples Federico II in Italy. The animals use that skill to find hidden food and to avoid becoming food themselves.

Kuba and his colleagues observed how three common octopuses (Octopus vulgaris) and four Mayan octopuses (Octopus maya) approached small holes. For each individual, the team measured the distance between the octopus’s eyes as an indicator of the size of their most rigid cartilage around their brain. Then the researchers designed acrylic boxes with holes that were slightly smaller or larger than that eye-to-eye measurement. They plopped the octopuses inside and watched what happened.

Octopuses have slightly different escape how-tos, depending on the size of the hole they are squeezing through. Here, a common octopus (Octopus vulgaris) wriggles through a space just a little bit bigger than their most rigid body parts. It takes just three steps for the octopus to free itself from the acrylic box.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists

Common octopuses used one of two escape strategies depending on the hole’s size. When the hole was wider than the distance between their eyes, the octopuses pushed themselves through it in three steps. First, they snuck one or two arms through the hole and then threaded a couple more arms through. Finally, they used the arms that they had already snaked through the hole to push against the box and yank their head and the rest of their arms through in one fell swoop. The whole operation took a few seconds.

When the hole was narrower, common octopuses added a fourth step. They shoved all of their arms through the hole first and then squished their head and bulbous mantle through.

When a hole is smaller than their most rigid body parts, common octopuses add a fourth step to wrestle their bodies through an opening.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists

Mayan octopuses behaved more cautiously than the common octopuses. When confronted with the narrower hole, Mayan octopuses didn’t even attempt to fit inside of it. They usually ignored it. This difference between the species could stem from their biology or how they’ve adapted to their environments, Kuba says. Mayan octopuses live in sandy, rocky areas, so while they might disappear under rocks, they don’t often need to cram through holes, he says.

The team hopes these escape artists will inspire new soft robots that can morph their shape to fit through tiny spaces, says Wenci Xin, a robotics researcher at the National University of Singapore. “This incredible capability could enable robots to overcome environmental limitations and enter spaces that are difficult to reach.”

Studying how octopuses navigate different types of holes may provide additional clues for robots, Crook says. For instance, the cephalopods may take a different tack for openings that are more like slits or tubes than holes.

Currently, robots built to fit through tiny holes tend to be snake-shaped, but further research on these eight-armed contortionists could unlock other configurations.

#6328. The Sky Today on Saturday, November 7: Venus meets the Moon

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Venus is already primed to capture attention above the eastern horizon before sunrise. This morning, the Moon passes 1.1° due south of Earth’s sister planet at 7 A.M. EST.

You can easily catch the pair an hour before sunrise, some 6° high in the east and climbing as the sky begins to brighten. Magnitude –4.5 Venus blazes to the upper left of the delicate crescent Moon, whose western limb is just barely lit as the Sun sets across the lunar nearside. Look for earthshine on the already-shadowed portion of Luna’s face, as sunlight bouncing off Earth lights it up.

Near Venus is another bright light: This is Spica, Virgo’s alpha star, shining at magnitude 1.0 and also lingering in the morning twilight. This morning it lies 1.3° northeast of Venus, with the planet and star roughly side by side above the horizon. Use this view as an anchor point: By the 10th, Venus will have moved to stand due west of this star and will be located to its upper right.

#6327. Researchers get their best look yet at an 850-year-old star explosion featuring massive chains of gas that look like pearls

Debris around the surviving star of the 1181 supernova forms chains of giant knots, and the star lies almost exactly at its center.

A supernova usually marks the end of a star. In 1181, Japanese, Chinese and Arabic astronomers recorded one that wasn’t quite the end: a scorching leftover star, now ringed by long, straight streaks of gas.

New telescope images show those streaks aren’t smooth. They’re chains of knots, each one wide enough to hold Neptune’s orbit about ten times over.

The images also put the surviving star almost exactly at the center of the debris. A centered star means the blast gave it almost no push, a clue to how the explosion played out.

Tim Cunningham of the University of Warwick led the work with Ilaria Caiazzo of the Institute of Science and Technology Austria. Cunningham did the research while at the Harvard & Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics.

Astronomers call the debris cloud Pa 30, and it’s the only one of its kind known in the Milky Way.

Observers in three cultures noted down the explosion. Its remains weren’t identified until 2013, when volunteer sky watchers spotted an unknown cloud in archived infrared images. The cloud was later tied to the old record; it lies about 7,500 light-years from Earth.

The star that exploded was a white dwarf, the dense, Earth-sized core a star leaves behind once it has used up its fuel.

In an interview with Earth.com, Caiazzo explained why something survived. “The supernova that created Pa 30 was a Type Iax supernova, a peculiar kind of explosion in which a white dwarf is not completely destroyed, leaving behind a partially burned stellar remnant,” she said.

The leftover star is extremely hot, about 360,000°F (200,000°C). It also blows out a wind at roughly 10,000 miles per second (16,000 kilometers per second).

Most supernova debris is a churned-up mess. Pa 30 looks more like a burst of fireworks, with straight streaks pointing out from the center. An earlier study found the gas has been flying outward at a steady speed since the explosion.

“No other known supernova remnant shows such long, straight filaments; most have a much more chaotic structure,” Caiazzo said. “Understanding how these filaments formed is one of the big open questions about Pa 30.”

To get a sharper look, the team used the Gemini North telescope on Mauna Kea in Hawaii. In mid-2025, the telescope gathered nearly seven hours of images. Its filters passed only the light that glowing sulfur and oxygen give off.

The sulfur images showed about ten times as many streaks as earlier pictures had. Up close, most streaks broke into a string of knots.

Each knot is about 60 billion miles (100 billion kilometers) across. The knots are similar in size along each streak and from one streak to the next. Their spacing looks fairly regular too.

The oxygen glow, faint and fuzzy in earlier images, turned out to come from the same streaks as the sulfur.

The knots give modelers something new to match. One idea is that the streaks rippled where fast-moving debris slid past thinner gas, and that the gas then cooled and clumped.

Another, in which the star’s wind shaped the streaks, has trouble explaining why the debris moves outward so steadily.

“We have now discovered that the filaments are not smooth, but are instead made up of individual knots,” Caiazzo said. “That gives us an important new clue about how the explosion unfolded and how the ejected material evolved afterward.”

Computer simulations of this kind of explosion often start the blast off to one side of the white dwarf. A lopsided blast should push the surviving star the other way. Simulations predict speeds of up to about 370 miles per second (600 kilometers per second).

“Because momentum has to be conserved, an asymmetric explosion should give the surviving star a ‘kick’ in the opposite direction – much like an astronaut throwing an object in one direction and being pushed the other way,” Caiazzo told Earth.com.

The team traced where the streaks point back to. The cloud’s center matched the star’s position almost exactly, so the star’s sideways speed can’t be more than about 9 miles per second (14 kilometers per second).

If the push could have gone in any direction, its total speed is almost certainly below about 60 miles per second (94 kilometers per second).

“That tells us that it cannot have received a large kick, and therefore that the explosion must have been actually quite symmetric,” Caiazzo said.

The knots are only barely sharp enough to measure. Streaks that overlap along the line of sight also make their spacing hard to pin down.

The star’s motion toward or away from Earth hasn’t been measured directly. Spectra so far cover only about a tenth of the cloud.

What blew up in the first place is still open. Researchers have proposed two white dwarfs merging, and Caiazzo said the other possibility is a white dwarf pulling material from a companion star.

Her team now has observing programs on the James Webb and Hubble space telescopes. Combined with simulations, she said, those images could show what the system looked like before 1181 and what the surviving star will become.

Cunningham said similar remains of exploding stars may still be hiding in the Milky Way, since reliable records go back only about a thousand years.

Explosions of this type also show up as points of light in distant galaxies, but Pa 30 is the one close enough to study in this detail.

The full study was published in the journal The Astrophysical Journal.

The Vikings are famous for being warriors, but how frequently did Viking women take part in battles?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Vikings were explorers, farmers, merchants and, most famously, warriors who launched raids across large parts of Europe.

Stereotypes of Vikings usually conjure up images of muscular men. But over the past few decades, researchers have turned their attention to women of the Viking Age (roughly A.D. 793 to 1066) and the roles they held. For instance, there are stories of "shield maidens" who fought alongside men, and some of these texts mention Viking women who fought in battle. The archaeological record also holds evidence, including graves of Viking Age women who were buried with war-grade weapons and shields.

It's still a matter of debate whether women who lived during the Viking Age could be warriors, but this discussion raises another question: It's one thing to have texts describing female fighters and archaeological records of women buried with weapons, but what can the evidence tell us about how frequently Viking women fought in battle?

The answer, experts told Live Science, largely depends on our interpretation of texts, artifacts, and burials of Viking Age women, which often face higher scrutiny than burials of men who were buried with similar (or even fewer) weapons.

The Vikings used a runic system of writing, but they left precious few texts behind. Instead, much of what we know about the Vikings was written about them by people from other cultures or by their Norse descendants.

One of the most evocative texts was written in the 12th century by the Danish historian and theologian Saxo Grammaticus. In "Gesta Danorum" (Latin for "History of the Danes" and translated by Jenny Jochens), he wrote that "there were once women in Denmark who dressed themselves to look like men and spent almost every minute cultivating [combat] skills." As "if they were forgetful of their true selves they put toughness before allure, aimed at conflicts instead of kisses, tasted blood, not lips, sought the clash of arms rather than the arm's embrace, fitted to weapons hands what should have been weaving, desired not the couch but the kill, and those they could have appeased with looks they attacked with lances."

Another text about the Vikings, the medieval Irish "Cogadh Gaedhelre Gallaibh" ("War of the Irish with the Foreigners"), refers to a woman known as the "Red Lady" leading a Viking fleet in a raid on Belfast in the 10th century.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

There's a lot of uncertainty, said Neil Price, an archaeology professor at Uppsala University in Sweden who has written extensively about the Vikings. The text in the "Cogadh Gaedhel re Gallaibh" that refers to the Red Lady is of debatable accuracy, Price told Live Science in an email.

He suspects that Viking women fought in battle but not frequently. In addition, "female warriors were probably a very small minority," Price said.

A modern-day reenactment depicting Viking warriors.

The account written by Saxo Grammaticus is also contentious. Thomas Kristian Heebøll-Holm, a history professor at the University of Southern Denmark, said Saxo Grammaticus is not a reliable source.

"Saxo Grammaticus does write about female warriors, but only in the parts of his work concerned [with] the legendary past of Denmark," Heebøll-Holm told Live Science in an email. "Furthermore, these writings are not accurate, but moral and fictitious," Heebøll-Holm said, noting that, in some instances, Saxo Grammaticus seemed to be drawing on the stories of the Amazons, a group of legendary female warriors whom the ancient Greeks believed in with stories about them dating back more than 2,500 years.

Archaeological evidence can also be challenging to interpret. Archaeologists know of about 30 Viking Age female burials containing weapons, including three with swords in Scandinavia. Even more Viking Age women's graves have items that could have been used as weapons ‪—‬ including spears, axes and knives ‪—‬ although these tools also could have been used for hunting or tending to farms. Either way, we can't be sure if these women fought in battle.

"The first concern is that the weapons were really used by the deceased and were not merely included as signs of special status or social rank acquired through inheritance," Deborah Shepherd, an independent researcher who holds a doctorate in archaeology and has studied the Vikings extensively, told Live Science in an email. She noted that graves are often not well preserved, making it difficult to gather information.

This 1889 illustration shows a grave at Birka in Sweden. It is now known that the person buried with war-grade weapons and riding gear is a woman.

There were likely "some few female warriors, but they were probably only found in the highest ranking families, and their warrior career was probably short-lived," Shepherd said. "They wouldn't have fought in the great armies of later centuries but possibly did fight in pre-Christian skirmishes." (The Vikings began gradually converting to Christianity between the ninth and 12th centuries.)

There is at least one known case of a Viking woman found with what may be combat-related injuries. A Viking woman found in Solør, Norway, had a head injury consistent with a sword strike. She was 18 or 19 at the time she died, was buried with weapons and lived around 900.

Ole Kastholm, a curator and senior researcher at the Roskilde Museum in Denmark, said there is a lot of uncertainty regarding how frequently Viking Age women fought in battle.

Weapons "do occur as a grave good in a handful of graves with female human remains," Kastholm told Live Science in an email. "Often it is just a single weapon [such] as a spear or [a] battle axe. But we know of at least one example of a female grave with a full set of weapons as well as riding equipment," which is located in Birka, Sweden.

"If this was a man's grave, researchers would have no doubt that it was a warrior grave, and this explanation must necessarily also apply when the interred is a woman," Kastholm said.

That said, there were female warriors in other cultures. "One can also note in passing that female warriors were an almost common feature of central Asian societies for at least a millennium before the Viking Age," Price wrote in his book, "The Sea-King and the Sorceress: Life and Death in the Viking Age" (Basic Books, 2026).

For instance the Scythians are a people who flourished in eastern Europe and Asia and Scythian women have been found buried with horses and weapons. In some cases, the Scythian women suffered combat wounds such as arrowheads and it's been speculated that they may have been an inspiration for stories of the Amazons.

#6325. Scientists discovered a tiny furry predator from 165 million years ago that hunted slippery prey in the water

This Jurassic mammal relative swam like a platypus and hunted with three-rooted fangs, and its throat was ready for swallowing and nursing.

In most pictures of the dinosaur age, early mammals and their relatives are tiny creatures keeping out of the way. Many did weigh just a few grams.

One of those relatives was a swimming predator that weighed a few pounds and hunted with fangs anchored by three roots each.

The animal’s throat bones were the bigger surprise. They carried the anchor points for muscles that today’s mammals use to swallow, drink and nurse, which puts key parts of the modern mammal throat long before modern mammals existed.

The animal, named Megacauda sungei, comes from rock in Inner Mongolia, China, that formed in the middle of the Jurassic period, when dinosaurs dominated life on land.

That rock is between 163 and 168 million years old. Scientists know the animal from a single skeleton, now held by the Paleontological Museum of Liaoning.

Researchers from Shenyang Normal University, Shandong University of Science and Technology, the University of Chicago and the University of Bonn described it. Thomas Martin of Bonn, Zhe-Xi Luo of Chicago and Chang-Fu Zhou of Shandong led the work.

Megacauda belonged to the docodonts, an extinct group of animals closely related to true mammals. The name means “big tail,” after its broad, flat tail.

The team estimated it weighed between 2.2 and 4.4 pounds (1 and 2 kilograms). That makes it the largest known mammal relative from the Jurassic.

It was about twice the weight of its closest known relative, and 150 to 200 times heavier than a tiny docodont found in the same area.

The upper canine teeth stood about 60 percent taller than the lower ones, and each had three roots, a setup that no known mammal shares. Grooves and ridges along those fangs likely strengthened them for puncturing prey.

Farther back, the cheek teeth had blade-like points that sliced past each other, much like the teeth of seals. The team thinks Megacauda was a major predator that ate salamanders, fish and small water creatures without backbones.

The skeleton shows a body made for water. The tail was wide and flattened, with an outline closer to a giant otter’s than to the rounded tail of a beaver or platypus.

The hind feet were long, with long outer toes like those of a platypus or a sea otter. Its hip carried the kind of muscle attachments a platypus uses to hold its legs close to its body when it swims.

Up front, the limbs had features for digging. The team concluded that it lived much like a platypus does, hunting in water and sheltering in burrows on land.

Megacauda probably wasn’t as strong a swimmer as an otter or a beaver. Its tail muscles didn’t extend as far down the tail as they do in modern swimmers, so its tail likely gave it less push.

The rarest part of the fossil is the roof of the throat. CT scans showed the bones in three dimensions, including a small, bony hook at the back of the skull.

In marsupials and placental mammals, a muscle wraps over that hook and tightens the soft palate, the flexible back of the roof of the mouth. That firm palate gives the tongue something to press against when a baby suckles milk or an adult drinks.

A groove beside the hook likely anchored a second muscle. In living mammals, that muscle pulls the throat up against the soft palate during swallowing, sealing food and drink off from the nose.

Saddle-shaped bones under the throat, like those in many living mammals, completed the set.

Alongside the modern-looking hook, the skull kept older ridges seen in earlier mammal relatives.

Muscles don’t fossilize, so the team rebuilt them from where they attach in living animals, including an opossum. Based on that, they think the swallowing, drinking and nursing equipment arrived together, not one piece at a time.

Other docodonts lived in trees or burrowed underground like moles. Over about 100 million years they spread across the northern continents. Megacauda is the earliest known case of a mammal relative living partly in water.

“This shows how widespread docodonts were in the Northern Hemisphere and that this diverse group of animals developed very different lifestyles at an incredibly early stage,” Martin said.

The same mix of swimming and digging turned up again about 120 million years later, in an extinct group of mammals called pantolestids. About 30 million years after that, it arose once more in the group that includes otters and weasels.

Every conclusion here rests on one animal. The weight is an estimate from its skull and from similar-sized platypuses, and the soft palate and throat muscles are inferred from bone.

Whether Megacauda actually nursed its young, or how often it drank, can’t be read from bone alone.

Answering that would take more docodont fossils with their throats intact, along with the feeding structures of the earliest mammals for comparison.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.

#6324. How the Antigravity 360 Drone Will Change Your Travels

Drones are huge. And, while there’s lots of restrictions around them, a lot of travelers take them on road because they produce some amazing sweeping aerial shots.

There’s lots of amazing brands out there but one that I think is super cool is the Antigravity A1. Released in late 2025, attempts to render the traditional gimbal obsolete for a vast segment of creators. By leveraging a dual-lens 360-degree capture system, the A1 records everything in every direction simultaneously. The result is a “fly now, frame later” experience that feels less like piloting a drone and more like directing a virtual camera in a pre-recorded digital environment.

I was sent one to use and want to share my experience and why I like this product so much.

What make’s Antigravity 360’s so special is the two lenses. Most drones feature a single lens that points forward. However, the A1 features two ultra-wide-angle lenses positioned on the top and bottom of the central fuselage that each captures a 200-degree field of view. When those images are combines, they overlap to create a seamless 360-degree sphere.

And, in the final exported footage, the drone itself is digitally removed, creating the illusion of a camera floating in mid-air with no visible means of support.

The sensors themselves are 1/1.28-inch CMOS units. While smaller than the 1-inch sensors found on some “Pro” level photography drones, they are massive compared to typical 360 action cameras. This allows for significantly better low-light performance and a higher dynamic range, capturing details in the highlights and shadows that would typically be lost in the harsh contrast of a midday sun.

Most countries require drones weighing 250 grams or more to be registered and subject to stricter flight rules. Antigravity clearly understood the importance of this threshold because they made the A1 to weigh exactly 249 grams with its standard battery meaning it’s not considered a commercial drone so you don’t have to register it.

And the drone feels remarkably sturdy. It utilizes a high-grade carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer that offers a better strength-to-weight ratio than the standard ABS plastic found in cheaper models. The folding mechanism is satisfyingly tactile, clicking into place with a precision that suggests long-term durability. When folded, the drone is roughly the size of a large smartphone, though about three times as thick.

The Vision Goggles: These are sleek, lightweight, and feature dual 4K micro-OLED displays with a 120Hz refresh rate. The latency is nearly non-existent and they have integrated head tracking. Because the drone is recording in 360 degrees, you aren’t limited to seeing what is in front of the drone. When you turn your head to the left, the goggle feed pans to the left. If you look down, you see the ground passing beneath you. This provides a sense of presence and spatial awareness that is simply impossible with a traditional fixed-camera drone.

The drone uses a single-handed motion controller. You point the controller where you want to go and pull the trigger to accelerate. Tilt your wrist left to bank, or raise the nose of the controller to climb. It is an incredibly intuitive system that allows even a novice to fly through complex environments within minutes. For professional FPV pilots who prefer the precision of manual acrobatic flight, the A1 does support a traditional “Mode 2” stick controller, but the motion controls are so fluid that most users will likely never switch back.

The marketing for the Antigravity 360 proudly displays “8K Resolution.” In a traditional camera, 8K means every pixel is packed into a 16:9 rectangle. In 360 video, those pixels are spread across a full sphere. When you “reframe” that 8K sphere into a standard flat video, you are looking at a “crop” of the total image.

The color science is noticeably improved over previous 360 cameras. The A1 features a “Vivid” profile for those who want punchy, social-media-ready colors, and a 10-bit “Log” profile for professional editors who need to match the footage to other cameras in a color-grading suite. The stabilization, powered by Antigravity’s “FlowState” algorithms, is nothing short of miraculous. You can fly in 20mph winds, and the footage remains as steady as if the camera were on a tripod.

The “Antigravity Studio” app allows you to download footage wirelessly (at speeds up to 80MB/s) and reframe your video using your phone’s gyroscope. You simply watch the video and move your phone around to “film” the scene in real-time. The app also features “Auto-Frame,” an AI tool that identifies subjects and automatically generates a cut that keeps them in focus. For a solo creator, this effectively provides a virtual camera crew that never misses a shot.

Battery technology remains the bottleneck for all small drones. The A1’s standard Intelligent Flight Battery provides a theoretical 24 minutes of flight. In real-world conditions with moderate wind and constant recording, expect closer to 19 or 20 minutes.

While 20 minutes sounds short, the “work per minute” is much higher than a traditional drone. Because you don’t need to re-fly a path to get different angles, a single 20-minute flight can yield the same amount of usable footage as three flights with a Mavic. For those who need more time, the “Pro Battery” (which pushes the weight over 250g) offers a staggering 39 minutes of flight time, though it does compromise the drone’s agility slightly.

In terms of flight dynamics, the A1 is a “cinewhoop” style flyer. It is stable and predictable rather than aggressive and twitchy. It has a top speed of roughly 36 mph, which is plenty for following bikes or cars, but it won’t keep up with a professional racing drone. The “Turtle Mode” is a life-saver; if you crash and end up upside down, the drone can flip itself over using its propellers, allowing you to take off again without a “walk of shame” to recover the aircraft.

The Antigravity 360 is a niche product that is rapidly becoming mainstream.

The Antigravity 360 (A1) is the most exciting drone I have tested. By removing the need for a gimbal and the stress of manual framing, it allows the pilot to focus on the one thing that truly matters: the story they are trying to tell.

While the image quality isn’t quite at the level of a high-end cinema drone, and the lenses are admittedly delicate, these are small prices to pay for the creative liberation the A1 provides. It bridges the gap between traditional cinematography and the immersive world of VR.

If you are a creator who is tired of the same old “drone shots” and want to push the boundaries of what is possible in the air, the Antigravity 360 is an essential addition to your toolkit.

#6323. Nov. 7, 1882: A Great Comet transforms astrophotography

In early September 1882, a comet was sighted from the Cape of Good Hope in South Africa. The comet brightened over the following weeks, reaching a magnitude of -2 on the 15th; at perihelion two days later, it was bright enough to be visible during the day. But at the time, David Gill, the director of the Cape Observatory, was busy observing minor planets Victoria and Sappho. It wasn’t until Oct. 12 that, his minor planet observations completed, he turned his attention to the comet and began photographing it.

Gill captured images of the Great Comet of 1882 on Oct. 12, 20, and 21, and Nov. 7, 13, and 14. The Nov. 7 shot was the one he would become famous for, though: It was not the first photograph of a comet, but rather would signal a change in astronomers’ uses of astrophotography. The photo was a 100-minute exposure, resulting an image that included stars to 10th magnitude and the comet’s 18-degree tail. Spurred by the large number of stars captured in his photo, Gill saw the potential for using astrophotography for star mapping and began the Cape Photographic Durchmusterung. (Durchmusterung means “close examination” or “scrutiny.”) The project would catalog nearly a half-million southern stars. Gill shared the successes of the program internationally, prompting the assembly of the world’s first major astronomical conference. As a result, astronomers worldwide began to move away from traditional, manual star mapping and towards more efficient and comprehensive photographic techniques.

Elisa Neckar is senior production editor of Astronomy magazine, and the editor of the Today in the History of Astronomy feature on Astronomy.com.

#6322. This armored amphibian once lived and hunted on the seafloor

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The ancient creature differs from all other known amphibians in its ability to tolerate saltwater

A Gerrothorax maritimus fossil unearthed in China was discovered in an ancient seabed, suggesting it's the first and only amphibian known to have lived in the ocean.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Most amphibians shrivel or suffocate in saltwater. But long ago, an oddball armored amphibian may have dwelled deep in the ocean.

Scientists have found evidence that an ancient amphibian with a flattened body and upturned eyes may have once stalked the seafloor. The animal, Gerrothorax maritimus, is the first ever amphibian known to have lived without access to land or freshwater, researchers report October 26 in Nature Ecology & Evolution.

G. maritimus, which lived 237 million years ago, was rather unlike today’s amphibians, which breathe and drink through their porous skin. The creature’s lifestyle was unimaginable for an amphibian, says Ryosuke Motani, a paleobiologist at the University of California, Davis. Of the more than 8,000 amphibians known today, none live solely in saltwater.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Motani and his colleagues inspected two well-preserved G. maritimus fossils from the late Triassic Period, which spanned roughly 237 million to 201 million years ago. Each creature measured around 70 centimeters, about as long as a skateboard, and was swathed in armor made of bony plates. The specimens appeared nearly identical to their closest relatives, other amphibians that dwelled in freshwater, Motani says. But the fossils’ location was unusual: They were found in what was once a seabed, roughly 30 kilometers from any ancient land.

It wasn’t clear whether the creatures lived in the ocean or were landlubbers that got buried there after they perished. So the team performed a chemical analysis. Levels of different forms of strontium in the fossil bones matched those of the Triassic ocean. This telltale sign revealed that G. maritimus ate seafood and drank seawater. “That means it lived there,” Motani says.

For amphibians, “this is the first time that that we have hard evidence that they were actually adapted for long-term life in the sea,” says Lachlan Hart, a paleobiologist at the University of New South Wales in Sydney who was not involved with the new study. Hart and his colleagues previously suggested that a different ancient amphibian may have been seafaring but probably did not dwell in the ocean.

Scientists have long searched for a marine amphibian. The fossil record is littered with skeletal fragments revealing how some mammals, reptiles and birds have adapted to a salty lifestyle. “Amphibians were always the problem because they did not really follow the rule,” Motani says.

The same skin that makes today’s amphibians vulnerable to disease and toxins also makes saltwater fearsome. Key adaptations allowed G. maritimus to skirt these issues. G. maritimus and its relatives evolved bony body armor, probably for defense. But these hard plates would have helped the seafloor dwellers prevent water loss. And unlike modern amphibians, which typically lose their internal gills after the larval stage, this creature and its close relatives retained a fishy breathing strategy suitable for life in the depths.

G. maritimus fossils hint that the animal lurked on the seafloor as an ambush predator. Its jaw lifted upward like a toilet seat so that it could unleash a suction attack on fish and other small creatures.

There may yet be other amphibians hiding in ancient oceans, environments ignored by paleontologists studying these creatures. “Because they’re amphibians, we would be looking for them in terrestrial freshwater environments,” Hart says. Perhaps there are more amphibians that have gotten their sea legs.

NASA's Swift Observatory went out in a blaze of glory this week, but it left behind millions of images of the universe that could fuel discoveries for decades.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Early Wednesday (Nov. 4), NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory fell out of space, burning up in the sky over Sumatra. It was a fitting, fiery end for a telescope that spent 22 years studying the most powerful explosions in the universe — and, even with Swift gone, its observations will continue to feed scientific curiosity for years to come.

Swift's most important contributions to astronomy are not exactly eye candy. Designed to swivel toward deep-space explosions at a moment's notice, Swift excelled at capturing bright, fleeting and faraway specks of light. The multiwavelength observatory was equipped with optical, ultraviolet (UV) and X-ray instruments, allowing it to catch cosmic bursts of energy across the electromagnetic spectrum, zeroing in on flares of light that other telescopes might miss.

One of its most significant detections was a gamma-ray burst — an incredibly bright blast, likely emitted by a giant star as it exploded in a supernova before collapsing into a black hole. Swift's famous image of GRB 221009A, or the BOAT ‪—‬ short for "brightest of all time" ‪—‬ looks like a speckled orange bull's-eye, caused by waves from the explosion rippling across space.

How the Swift Observatory saw the gamma-ray burst GRB 221009A, which may be the most energetic emission of this kind ever seen.

But Swift also took millions of observations of the nearby universe, including galaxies in our backyard. One of its most jaw-dropping images is this 24-hour exposure of the Andromeda galaxy (M31), located about 2.5 million light-years from Earth.

Andromeda is the closest major galaxy to ours, and it may be destined for a shared fate. Scientists suspect that Andromeda and the Milky Way are drawing closer together and might eventually collide. The merger would add Andromeda's roughly 1 trillion stars to our sky, though there probably wouldn't be any life left on Earth to appreciate it.

In Swift's view of our encroaching neighbor, captured with the observatory's ultraviolet instrument, tens of thousands of Andromeda's stars shine like sapphires set in a sparkling ring.

According to NASA, the observatory detected some 20,000 ultraviolet light sources in this image, captured over two months from May to July 2008. These sources include thousands of dense, hot star clusters scattered across Andromeda's 150,000-light-year-wide ring, as well as the distant galaxy M32 (seen as a bright orb of light to the bottom right of Andromeda's center).

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In visible-light images of Andromeda taken with ground-based telescopes, the galaxy's bright center bleaches out many of the fiery young stars that emerge in Swift's view. While Swift likely won't be remembered best for shimmering starscapes like this one, it's a powerful reminder that looking at familiar structures in a new light can change everything.
